CURIOUS FACT ABOUT VISION.

Dr. H. C. Stevens, of Seattle, reports ex- periments which shew that objects seen by indirect vision ordinarily appear larger in the right half of the field Of vision than in the left. With a smaller number of persons this is reversed. From these facts he deduces a possible origin of right and left-handed- ness. Bight-handedness, or its reverse, de- velops at about the age of seven months. Dr. Stevens suggests that they may, be due to the phenomena of vision just described. By a reflex effect the infant reaches after the objects best soen with the arm nearest to them.
The Examinee Saturday, August 8, l9OB.

div.head: BLOOD IN THE BODY.
div.p: THE BLOOD IN THE BODY.

It is extremely difficult to find out the exact quantity of. blood, in the human body. In some foreign countries they do not hang criminals, they decapitate them. * Now it oc- curred to some scientifie men that the best way to tell how much -blood is in the body would be to weigh a criminal just before his head was cut off, and then to weigh the head and trunk after the blood had drained out of them. The difference in weight would then be the weight of the blood in the body befere the _head was cut off. As the result of many observations of this kind it was found that the blood in the body is about 12'5 per cent. of .the entire weight- of the, body, that is to say, if a body weighs 1001 b. it contains about 121 b. of blood.

div.head: MEASURER OF STARLIGHT.
div.p: A MEASURER OF STARLIGHT.

Professor Joel Stebbins and Professor F. C. Brown have constructed a small selenium cell, which, when placed in the focus of a l2in. refracting telescope, causes measurable deflections of the needle of ,a galvanometer in response to the impact of light-waves from individual stars. The planet Mars -.gave a deflection of 9 -millimetrek the, star Alde- baran a - deflection of -34 millimetres, and even a fourth magnitude star, Gamma Arietis, caused , a visible deflection. It is hoped that by the. use of a specially sensi- tive galvanometer this- inethed -may be greatly improved, and that if certain disturb- ing influences, particularly temperature changes, can be eliminated, accurate mea- surements of starlight by means of selenium cells will become possible.

div.head: AUGUST METEORS.
div.p: AUGUST METEORS.

Astronomers look annually for a display of meteors from August fith to 11th. These August meteors appear to radiate from a point in the constellation Perseus, 'and are hence kuown as Perseids. Pppularly they have been called- the tears of §aint Latir- ence, whose day -falls on the; 10th. The facts with regard to these August meteors support the view now Held by many astronomers that meteors are in many eases parts of eometary systems. In some cases the comet has ceased -to be luminous, and is represented by a ring cif dark fragments of matter 'revolving round the sun. Even when the comet still exists it may be followed by a train of dark frag- ments. The orbit of the August meteors corresponds so closely with that of the comet known as 111. 1802 that there can be little doubt that they are parts of the same system.

div.head: LAKE -THAT TURNS RED. –
div.p: A LAKE -THAT TURNS RED. -

One of the natural • curiosities of Switzer- land is Lake Alorat, which turns blood red every tenth year. For centuries this freak was regarded by the Swiss with supersiitious dread, and not- until scientists turned their attention to the matter was -the belief in the supernatural partly removed. Even now soine of the more ignorant persist in regarding the omen as

ONE OF EVIL IMPORT. The reddish colour is given the water by a minute plant closely related to the red snow. Exo.:..ry tenth year this plant begins to propa- gate, and so quickly does it grow that in a short time the whole lake is a crimson tide. rile plant is so minute as not to be percepti- ble- without the aid of a microscope, and there was some foundation for the early be- lief that the lake-had turned into a sea of blood.

div.head: TREE TRUNKS AS FILTERS.
div.p: TREE TRUNKS AS FILTERS.

A well-known Austrian engineer, M. Pfister, is stated to have discovered a remark- able property of the trunks of trees, namely, that of retaining the salt of Sea water that has filtered through the trunk in the-direc- tion of the fibres. He has consequently con. stinctecl an apparatus designed to utilise this property in obtaining drinkable water for the use of ships' crews. This apparatus consists of a pump, which sucks up the sea water into a reservoir, and then forces it into the

FILTER FORMED BY THE TREE TRUNK. As soon as a certain pressuro, is reached, the water is seen at the end of from one to three minutes, accortling to the kind of wood used, to make its exit from the other extremity of the trunk, at first in drops and then in fine streams, the water thus filtered being drink- able, freed, in fact, from every particle of the usual salty taste which is such a draw- back to water obtained in the ordinary manner.

div.head: /NO ONE HAS EVER SEEN THE SUN.
div.p: /NO ONE HAS EVER SEEN THE SUN.

That no one has ever seen the sun is a cold scientific fact, and the reason is this r What we see shining in the sky is the sun's atmo7 sphere, a glowing -masstcf blazing gases which surrounds the sun itself to a depth of thou- sands of miles. What is inside these blazing envelopes we do not know; the most learned astronomers can only tell us that there is a uticleus which is infinitely hotter than the

FIERCEST OF FIERY FURNACES, and that it occupies about nine-tenthe of the total mass which we see. So, when you look at the- sun you see only the gases and the flames that envelop him. It is not impossible to express the marvellous power of the sun's heat, but it is impossible to comprehend it. The heat emitted by the sun in each second is equal to that which would result from the combustion of eleven quadrillions six hun- dred thousand milliards of tons of coal burn- ing at the same time.

THE FINSEN TREATMENT OF LUPUS. The Finsen method of treatment consist in the application of light to diseased areas of the skin. It is mainly used in the treat- ment of lupus vulgaris. Originally, Finsen :made use of the direct rays of the sun. But it has been found more convenient to nee artificial light, and one now employs a very powerful electric carbon-arc as a source of light. The rays from the arc lamp are focussed on to the part by means of a series of quartz lenses (quartz having the property of cutting off the heat rays to some extent), and a water-cooling ey s tein is employed. As a further precaution it is necessary, says the Iloepital, to remove the barrier to the pene- tration of the light rays which is offered by the red colouring matter of the blood in the tissues under treatment. This is effected by the employment of a water-cooled quartz compressor, which is kept constantly pressed en the part while the exposure is taking place.

div.head: LIQUEFACTION OF HELIUM._
div.p: LIQUEFACTION OF HELIUM._

Professor Onnes has persevered in his at- tempts to liquefy this most refractory of gases, and his efforts seem to have been really Crowned with success. So far as is at present known, says the GT obe, there are no score worlds to conquer in this direction: As. a general rule the difficulty of redhcing a gas to the liquid state has been found to increase as the atomic weight diminishes. Thus nitroc. gen, atomic weight 14, is mere difficult to liquefy than oxygen, atomic weight 16, and hydrogen, atomic weight 1, is more refrac- tory still. Yet helium, with an atomic weight of 2, has proved much more - difficult to I:quefy than the lighter hydrogen. _Dismiss- ing earlier attempts to liquefy helium, Sir J. Dswar concluded .the 'boiling-point of the liquid would be sdeg. 'absolute temperature, or 268 deg. Cent. below freezing point. The boiling-point of liquid hydrogen is 20.,5deg. oissolute. The great importance of the lane- action of helium is tiie• low temperature thereby attainable, which will • enable physi- eists to study matte:: under new conditions.l

div.head: FADED PRINTS.
div.p: FADED PRINTS.

One of the qtitticurf that frequently ccmes to me is how fade/prints may he mecle'vigprcus again. In veiy many cares this is difficult, and it is always impossible to give a single reply which will deal with all circum- stances, becatte different treatments are necessary for different papers. Generally, however, the prints which have faded are silver, in millet). the whites may have turned slightly yellow, and the itage has changed to a deep yellow or a yellow-brown. Generally, in such cases, the simplest way of proceeding is by copying the print in the camera, making anew negative and printing therefrom. Using ordinary plates without any light- tilter,it will be found that the yellow image photographs as strongly as if it were a black one, and that therefore the cepy is quite as good as the original was in its fresh condition.

div.head: HINT ON COPYING.
div.p: A HINT ON COPYING.

Probably all my readers know that there are tables of conjugate foci to be found in most of the genetal reference books on photography, and that these tell them what are the proper relative distances from the lens to the original, and from lens to plate in copying to any given proportion. Most of them also know that when copying to the same size as the original, the lens must be exactly mid way between the plate and the picture to be copied, and that its distance from each of them must be eqnal to twice its equivalent focus. The ()divalent focus, I need hardly say, is what is commonly spoken of as 'the focal length of the lens. When the copying is to be a little smaller than the original, the lens will be a little nearer tp the plate than to the original, and vice- vetsa, if the ciopying is to be an enlargement, the lens will be a little nearer to the original.than to the plate. Beginners in copying gcnerally fix their original and tl.eir camera, and then rack the lens in and out in the endeavour, to get sharpness and proper size. I think they will generally find it easier if they fix the position of the lens roughly where it will give the size of copy that they need, end then move the whole camera nearer to and farther from the object copied, keeping their beads under the focussing clot hand watching the ground glass. Ibis seems liken very simple and childish solu- tion of a dificulty, but I have known it net excellently in helping an amateur c, pyist who found great trouble in getting his proper enlargement with sharpness.

div.head: MOUNTING _FOII_XIIIBITIONS.
div.p: MOUNTING _FOII_XIIIBITIONS.

Large mounts for relatively small pictures are still fashionable, and amateurs often do not know exactly why these are used. I take it that the real reason is that the exhibitor thinks his pictures can be better appreciated from a little distance rather than when studied closely, and that a large mount has the tendency to induce the spectator to stand some distance army from the print. Generally speaking, the print is not mounted in the centre of the mount, but usually appre- ciably near the top than the bottom. The proportion which is best depends entirely upon the particular nature of the picture, the strength of its masses and so forth, but probably the very picture which needs a mount at all is improved by having the width below the print at least twice as great as the width above and at the sides. The greater space below tends to give support and dignity to the picture. . AUTOCHROMY.

Though the intense enthusiasm whieh existed about this process a few months ago has subsided, the amount of steady work that is being done in natural-colour photography is enormous, and there will be numbers of exhibitors showing work that may fairly be called pictorial in the form of 'autochrotre transparencies at the Exhibitions in the autumn. Ilessrs. Lumiere are giving a great help to the process by working out a method of development, and a dark room safe light which. enables -the developing process to ,be watched almost as easily as is the base with ordinary plates. Personally, I think that the time-development with insistence upon the necessity for exact exposure is better for securing high quality of weak, but I know that many amateurs will be only too glad to feel that they can watch development. rho dark-room light filter is of a green colour that is raoie comforting to the eyes than the ordinary ruby darkrroom light.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A SANKEY MAlc.—We regret to record the death, under tragic circumstances, of a well- known resident in the person of Mr. Arthur Cash, son of Mr. Robert Cash, nf Sandy-lane, Great Sankey. The deceased, who was 23 years of age, was killed at Clock- Face Colliery on Saturday morning at .bout ten o'clock. He was walking in the Power House, when he fell a distance of 13 feet, dropping on his head and breaking his neck. He *.as well known as an athlete' and had arranged to take part in sports to be held on Bank Holiday and Tuesday ard Wed- nesday of this week. Much sympathy is expressed with the parents in their td bereavement.— The inguest*was held on Wednesday by Mr. Brighouse. —Deceased had for some time held a licence as an amateur cyclist, and had raced at a number of local sports. Ills father gave him a very good character, and said that the death was a very sad blow to them. He worked for about six years with him ss a toolmaker, and for three years had been at this colliery.—Joseph Woods, crane-driver, of Oxley-street, Sutton, said that on Saturday they were putting a floor in the electric-power house. The floor was composed of steel girders and concrete, which rested on brick pillars about 13ft. high. Deceased had stooped down under a water-pipe which went across the place to prepare a bole in one of the pillars for the end of one of the-girders. When he had done this he jumped iff3 from his knees and caught his hack against the water pipe, which knocked him off the flooring, and be fell down into the cellar. The distance was only 13ft., but Cash unfortunately fell on his head. Witness and a man named Simpson picked him up, but by the time the ambulance was obtained he appeared to be dead. Dr. Davies, of St. Helens, soon arrived. but found be could do nothing.—A verdict of "Accidental 'death " was returned.

GARDEN ROBBERY AT PENRETR.—At the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, John Sheridan, Moss Bank, Whines, was fined 20s. and casts or one month for stAaling threepennyworth of apples from the orchard of William Webster, at PonLetb. On Sunday That the probecutor found prisoner crawling on his hands and knees in the garden. When discovered he made the excuse that ho wanted to buy fruit.

div.head: !Local
div.p: !Local
WOMEN'S CHAT.

Wet Weather Garments.—The- start for the country esuslly entails an over-hauling of wet vi °ether garraents. One goes awry Loping for the Lest in the matter of weather, but it is wise to he prepared for the worst. Unlike other RTOCIJS of the nate:rote, rubbered materials are never any better for a " rest cure," and for that reason especial care should he taken in putting away waterproof. If that vete alwass done, many would be saved the necessity for seeking something new in waterproofs at this.season of the year. The silky satin coats are meat in demand, but it perhaps ,:es well to choose something a little less dressy. Travelling Geer.—The modern tendency to do with less holiday luggage is not very aeparent in the head- gear of fashienable women, which we sometimes see going hither and thither about the country in hat boxes almost as large as the chest of drawers trunks, beloved of Americans. As a rule the woman of fashion insists upon keeping her hat boxes within sight,and it is there- fore fottunate for the general convenience of railway travellers, that not every woman wears hats as largo round as the hem of her skirt. Happily it is coming to be recognised that there are better was sof enjoying a holiday than spending all the time cn the fashionable seaside dress parade, and it is the "do as you like " kind of holiday that now appeals to the great majority of people. We are consequently able to do with less luggage, and for many of us the light cane or fibre cases suffice for our needs in this direction. If one has to take large trunks, those of the chest-of drawers descrip- tion certainly offer advantages in saving packing and crushing, and also the tiresome task pi unpacking. The Correct Angle.—When purchasing a hat, we are often pleased enough with the effect ,aben the black- satined young woman in the milliner's showroom places it upon our Lead, and when we beet it home we are very frequently disappointed, and at n loss to understand whet has happened to make our purchase less desirable. Of course the carefully manipulated mirrors end becomingly shaded rooms have something to do with it all, but it is usually more a question of angle than : anything else. The ecung et omen knows exactly how to place the hat upon our head, end we very frequently do not. 'the safest plan is to practice fixing the hat on in the showroomeand master the art of doing so, beret e coming to any decision. After being worn quite fist epee the bead, bats are again being raised at the tack, and slightly at ths left side, by means, of the old 1 familiar bandeau, and of course need match more careful poising than the list varieties. Fashion and tteelth.—The fiillyetticoat is still con- spicuous by its absence in the up-to-date trousseau, silk woven combinations and satin knickers having taken the place of cur one time more artistic nnderwear. It seems to be as important ite ever, that we should be slim, so • we are wearing as few clothes as possible, eating only what is guaranteed not to make us . fat, and taking as much outdoor exercise as possible. The I electors are unanimous in epenoving of tbemodes of the moment. Petticeals are Lest left alone they tail 'ten' knickers being much more healthy, then the crazes for eating less, and carefully, abstaining from alcohol, and staking up outdone games, are they say, and as we can readily understand, all to the good. Beautiful .Embroideries.—Early in the yeer, quantities of ordinary white pearl embroideries were utilized by leading dressmakers, but the white pearls have now taken place to coloured ones, such ornamentation , appearing upon coloured toilettes. There are pale pink, pale green, dull gold. or silver, and grey peall embroideries in evidence at the moment, and these look particularly well upon satin, chiffon end lace. The amateur should not end the task of building up these embroideries (on a simple scale) a difficult one, a , wonderful selection of all kinds of pearls being offered us, and divers ideas as to style and pattern can Le gleaned from exhibits in thenshop widows. A Convenient Notion.--Tlfe idea of having a little imp printed upon one's writing paper, and the back of ; one's cards, shevring the exact position of one's house, I whether situated in a net work of streets and squares, ; or in the depths of the country, is likely to prove a I boon and a blessing to those who have to ferret it out. ; A mere address is often distractingly vague, but the i map sets all this right. Notepaper s larger than it has I been for some seasons past and the one time favourite half-sheet is less in evidence. Probably this is due in great measure to the number of things we have inscribed ' upon the paper before we begin. There is, of course I the address, the monogram, and perchance the telephone number to be thought of, and if we live in the country there is the nearest telegraph office and station to mention. And now comes the little map to help to take up_space. Still few will regret this last addition, ! more especially when they sally forth to find a house: or flat with an address as vague and bewildering as it is , possible to make it. Christian Names by the Yard.—Lieutenant Leo de Orellana Tollemache, who announces that he has shed about half-a-dozen of his " appellatires " belongs to a ' family remarkable for its prolific indulgence in Christian names. He has an elder brother with fifteen or sixteen, and a younger sister with everimore. Her full name is Lyona Decima Veronica Esyth Cndine Cyssa Htlda Rowena Viola Idela Myra Ursula Isabel I Blanche Lelias Dysart Plantagenet Tollernache- I Tollernache. Her father the Rev. Ralph Tollernriche, I was evidently of the same opinion as tie parents who gave their daughters a long string of Christ len names, in order that the future husbands might have ua diffi- culty in choosing the one they liked best. A Minimum Wage for Home-Workers.--It is sixty- five years since Thomas Flood wrote " The Song of the Shirt," and as yet little has been done to ameliorate the lot of the under-paid home worker, If, however, legislation follows nyon the lines recommended by Sir Thomas Whittaker's Committee on Home Work, it should go far to save young women end girle from the evils of sweating. In spite of public sympathy with the movement for securing a fair day's wages for a fair day's work, there are thousands of such home workers engaged in making shirts ,at tenpence a dozen, and blouses at a few pence each. That is the kind of thing for which the Committee recommend preventive measures, confining legislation in the first instance to home-workers engaged in the tailoring. shirtmaking, undercloth.ng and baby-linen trades. Wages Boards would be appointed, composed of employers and employed, in these particular trades, who would fix a minimum wage, and any employer paying or offering less, would be open to penalties. This would, no doubt, make the selling prices in the shops a little mere but the public would not raise an outcry against thrit, if something effectual were done to improve the piteous lot of the sweated home-worker. Dancing.—The modern dance has become something very like a "ron-p" paying little regard to artistic effect. The minuet of our grandmother's time has gone, and so the old-fashioned quadrille and most of the set dances. It is therefore to be feared that the efforts of of the Imperial Society of Dance Teachers, to inspire n little more grace in the ballroom, will not he very successful. The Society has been discussing dancinr, in all its aspects, at a Congress in London, and it is ' evident from its high-sounding title that it regards the subject of much importance. So it is from the point of view that dancing is universal, and that there is not a cation or a people civilized or uncivilised, who do cot indulge in this pleasure in some form or other. But in these latter days we have become more boister- eme in our dancing and as in our games, partly no doubt because elderly people have come to regard it as exclu- sively for the young and seldom do more than make a pretence of taking part in it.
MADGE.

div.head: WHAT A STOUT WOMAN
div.p: WHAT A STOUT WOMAN
SHOULD WEAR.

It, is a mistake for a fat woman to wear long, loose, sweeping gowns. She should wear sell-fitted clothes, and choose dark materials," said a dressmaker notable for making "good figures" of at, nt women. "3ly success with stout women, however, is principally dile to the fact that I can make them in reality slender if they Will take my advice. I advise them invariably to go to their chemist,and get one half-ounce of Marmola, one ounce of fluid extract of Glycyrrhiza B.P.,rne ounce of pure Glycerine MP., and Peppermint Water to make six ounces in all. The mixture should be taken (a dessertspoonful to a dose) after meals and at bedtime. " All these are simple, wholesome remedies that cannot do harm to anyone. They greatly improve the health, while the rapid decrease of fat is truly astonish- ing. I have known a woman to lose over thirty pounds between visits to me. It takes the fat off symmetrically. too, without causing wrinkles, does not interfere with the diet in any way, and does not necessitate a lot of fatiguing exercise to assist results. I wonder more dressmakers do not try this plan of mine, for the ingredients are cheap, easily procured, and pleasant to take, end, as I said, really improve one's health and appearance. 1

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME,
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME,
DIRECTOIRE MODE.

The Directoire fashions have US yet made slow headway, but signs are not lacking to shew that they will flourish during the next few months and be quite firmly fixed in favour by Christmas. Then, says a' writer in 31.A.P., we shall never want to abandon them, for if we are not exactly the first by whom the new is tried, we are cer- tainly loth to part with old favourites. _How re- luctantly we abandoned the short coat; with what tenacity do most of us still stick to the short sleeve! By the time our womenfolk and —almost as important—our menfolk have re- turned from Aix. and Homburg, and Marien- bad, their eyes will be quite habituated to the new outlines, and, late October in town is sure to show us many radical changes.

div.head: DAINTY FROM
div.p: A DAINTY FROM

Pictured in our sketch is a delightfully dainty little " best " frock for summer wear. This pretty dress is 'carried out in fine. white spotted muslin of good quality, and will wash and wear admirably. At the neck the f rock's is cut cut in V-shape, and is edged with a' band of Valen- ciennes insertion. Vrorri the shoulder to the levy' of the point of this band of insertion all the fulness of the frock is set in a succession of small perpendicular tucks, which are crossed at intervals by bands of Valenciennes insertion

rather narrower than the band at the neck. From the lowest band the frock falls in pretty soft, full folds, and is finished r.t the bottom by a gathered frill of the muslin edged with nar- row Valenciennes lace. Inside the V-shaped opening at the neck comes a dainty little vest of finely-tucked white muslin, finished with a minute frill at the top. The sleeves are simple full three-quarter affairs made without lining, and set into a little cuff of Valenciennes insertion. THE USEFUL RUCHED HAT.

Fdll.- this mid-season a good many- hats are being worn with a very high, thick ruche of tulle round the crown for their only trimming: These are very becoming, and; considering how simple they are, they are wonderfully smart. Above all, they have the great advantage that for a round of country visits it is very easy to take several ruches, so that the 'hat can be freshly trimmed if it should become draggled or wet. This is a revival of a fashion of two or three years ago, when everyone wore ruches round the crown. The tulle used should be very fine and very thickly pleated: It is quite smart when the ruche has raw edger,- but if it is made of doublo tulle it is possible ,to make it last kinger, by pul- ling it out with the fingers, and, as it were, pushing the outside of each pleat into the inside cf. the next. A SMART NEW HAT.

Just at present there exists a perfect furore for ribbon-trimmed hats of every kind, and it is probable that this type of chapeau will be the smartest headgear for the next two or three months. In our sketch is pictured a particu- lairly attractive model, which is principally trutnsed with wido and very soft satin ribbon in a loveiy tone of wistari. mauve. The hat itself is large, and is carried out in straw of a pretty

purple tone, edged with an inch-wide border of deep ivory, almost biscuit, straw. The crown is entirely made of the finest point d'esprit net in exactly the same tone as th 6 straw which bor- ders the. brim, and is very closely gathered, so that it stands up in delightfully crisp fashion. Round the base of this crown the ribbon is lightly twisted, the hat being, finished by count- less loopings of tho ribbon massed on the left side. side. A WORKER FOR PEACE.

The Peace Congress reminds Us, says "Mir- anda" in the Lady's Pictorial, of those notable women-workers who have ranked among the pacificist party, a party that has not been popu- lar as far as English;-omen are concerned. For women peace-leaders we have to look further afield, abroad and in the Colonies. One of the women whb has done much for the world's peace ia Miss Jessie Ackermann. whose labc.rs in connection with the UniVersal Peace- Associa- tion have made her name a household word in the United States. Of Miss Ackermann'a rower to draw an audience ,sorric ittea may be got from the fact that, when she was giving a series of lectures in an Australian town last year, tho doors had to be guarded by police to prevent overcrowding by too eager hearers. Miss Ackermann believes that more is being done for Peace in the South American Republies—those former hotbeds of fighting—than anywhere else, and she pays a cordial tributa to the efforts of the women of Chili and Argentina to pro- mote that perpetual truce now established be- tween the two States.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RuclrE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RuclrE.

APRICOT CittrtsE.--Fruit 'chce9es have become , almost indispensable after-dinner sweetiveats nowadays. the mere fact that from the 'original damson to 'ginger and mulberry and cherry to raspberry cheese a variety of different kinds has become essential to dessert resulting in much resolution on the part of those whose kitchen gardens are beyond reproach. According to a capital old recipe, says the Evening Standard, a good way of preparing the apricots was to stone them, and afterwards boil them until reduced to ha pulp, and then rub all but 1t ho skins through a sieve, returning th fruit meanwhile to the fire, and by degrees stirring into the saucepan a pound and two ounces of sugar to every pound of pulp. When it has all been added, •stirring should be continued over the fire, the greatest care being, howewr, exercised to keep the paste from boiling. Be-fore it reaches boiling-point it .thould 'therefore, he taken rdE the fire, the paste scraped to one side of the saucepan, and allowed to 11001 a little, when it may be divided into 'van- Cu. shapes, placed on a fireproof dish, and dusted with sugar, or pressed into raoukla and sa in a cool oven to drs.,

div.head: CREATURE IMPULSE.
div.p: A CREATURE IMPULSE.
[ALL. RIGHTS RESERVED.]
By G. B. BURGIN,
1 tutho'r '-of "The Shatters of Silence," "A Wilful Woman," "Tuxter's Little Maid," "His Lord- ship and Others," "The Judge, of the Four 1 Corners," ,

"Whir—r--r! Whir—r—r Whir—rt!" The breath of the Destroyer smote the back of lais neck, a strong hand clutched him, pulled aim violently towards 1113 ditch as something !truck his shoulder, and Douglas Home was east into the brambles. The steam-tram silently climbed the hill without deigning to notice its victim. Whereupen, Home scranibk.id out of the ditch and gave sorrow words—Anglo4iaxon words.

•• He crawled up to the, top of the hill and gazed at St. Prude° in the valley below, ills knapsack galled him; he was hungry; tired, thirsty;, and the lights in the little village looked inviting. How his head • ached! The weird gloaming leyessed him; he wanted to get away from it, to foregather with folk. This narrow escape from being cut in two-by the tramway engine made him think dully of the precariousngss of existence. - He felt Boer sharpshooters pinging at him -as, he dragged poor Featherstone's boa), away from the melee. Who was it pulled him aside a's the engine came upon him unawares? .oh, yea; this blue-eyed, tall, slim girl ,in knickers. Ho was annoyed that a Frenchwoman With Englishrloolting blue eyes should have -saved him from a train engine. He Abhorred knickers —for girls. Before he could stammer his thanks to the girl, she mounted her bicycle like ati athlete, and, with a few rin t, gin words in French, 'whirled away through the gloaming. In the midst of his confusion, he felt grateful,to her for not exposing the badness of his French. He had come abroad with thb, idea that any kind of French was good enough for Brittany. Ugh! The growing bruise on his shoulder warned him what would have happened had not the girl pulled him away from that monster. Ho was quite unprepared for such consideration from a stranger. But -that train engine Ah, if he could only upset that!: • "Just like the French," he muttered. "What other nation would seek to slay the tourist on whom it lives,. by having steam-engines which cross the road in the gloaming and collie upon one with hardly a sound? Pouf! As they say here, that was a narrow shave. • tlow am I to get ,even with the girl for saving my life ? What, would they say in -Fleet-street, i my- mangled remains had been found in an obscure corner of Brittany ? The fellows would feel annoyed that a war Correspondent had come to so ,untimelir an.end. On second_ thoughts "—he ruefully- surveyed his knapsack, in which the engine had torn a hole— "it would annoy-me .He, moved towards the valley, having once more recovered. "tone:" Not -even the ghostly 'purr of a Whirling windmill's sails Could startle him now. "What right," he Muttered, lhnping lamely ,down the hill—"what right has a French girl to such beautiful eyes ? And she needn't have hurried away without waiting to be thanked. No repose about French people. Always in a hurry. . Perhaps she wanted to get home to dress for dinner." ' , , _

„ . He-entered the little triangular market-place of St. Prudoe and made his way to the nearest inn. No one seemed' particularly al-Axil:nag to welcome him. People were busy moving tables and chairs fro:n tae big dining-room. ' He banged on the door until Madame 1-)amerre appeared. Madame was voluble apologetic. ."Alas ! that monsieur should think her neglectful when she loved le,s Avkis so much; but everyone was preparing for the dance.” Monsieur was glad that she loved him' but he was not interested in the dance. Could he have a bed and some dinner—the dinner first, the bed afterwards

But certainly. Monsieur must not worry himself. Monsieur was wounded. If Monsieur Would have the goodness to lean on her she would shew him to his moth, and get him a nice little dinner in the bar-parlour. The ordinary moth was being prepared for the ball. Monsieur had met with an adventure ?

Monsieur had met- With a stearnrengioe which had foully and treacherously sought to slay him unawares. He had done 'nothing to the steam- engine, although it seemed to resent his arrival at St. Prudoc.
Doubtless it lacked sympathy, Madame Lamerre hastened to remark. If Monsieur would give himself the pain to make himself comfortable— Ah ! there li,as Marie with the hot water.

Monsieur "gave himself the pain," and the motherly old Frenchwomm helped him upstairs, presented him with a stiff glass of cognac, and, stripping off his shirt, in spite of Home's protests' applied soothing unguents to the big, black, broken-skinned welt across his shoulder. Then she ra-dressed him, put his arm in a sling, and looked at her work. "I do not understand how Monsieur comes to have his arm so.pearly dislocated ?"

"It was the girl," Home explained. "She must have whirred up on her bike and jerked me away st as if she had been tailing a bull on the Pampas. I—l was in a brown study." Madame did not understand about tailing bulls, but she helped Home downstairs into the bar-parlour, and gave him the best dinner he had had for years. "You mustn't take so much trouble with me," he protested, after having eaten his fill. "You are too kind."

"Mail "said Madame. "Monsieur fails to comprehend. It is for the honour of France. Monsieur does not understand that the steam- engine has disgraced us as a na,tion." - Home felt annoyed when the door opened and a rush of chilly September air filled the room. "Come in, mother,". said an. unmistakahly English voice, "or we shall be late. I nearly sprained my wrist pulling that—" The girl stopped suddenly, for Home had risen to his feet, his handsome brown eyes aglow. "So you're not Frreneh after all!" he cried. "I knew it; I knew it!"

• The girl looked at him doubtfully. "No, lam not French," she said, slowly. "May I ask the reason of this sudden accession of patriotism on Your part ? " Her cloak slipped to the floor as -she spoke, and she stood revealed in all the beauty of sweet one-and-twenty. • To his great delight, Home noticed that she no longer wore the disfiguring knickers. A soft, filmy blue dress set off her ethereal beauty.. She had exquisite blue eyes, yellow hair, sweet lips, even white teeth, straight nose, not too small, And shoulders such as one sees in dreams. Mammn, behind her, was the same, with the portliness of twenty additional summers. • She had a frank, handsome face, and Surveyed Home with sympathy as an Englishman in a. strange land who had been wounded by unsympathetic steam-engines. He was even handsomer than the-girl. Tall, dark, athletic, with clear brown eyes .and a moustache which had not long encountered the vicissitudes of the world; it seemed to need support. „ . „.. . .

"I think," said 'mamma, "that my daughter had the pleasure of--" She paused. . The girl ruefully looked at Home. "And so I can't get my glove on to-night; ?." "Douglas Home." "W—what!" cried mother and daughter together. "The Douglas Home ?". Here the girl added,' softly:•"The hero ! __
_ Home -blushed beneath his tan. "of course I'd no business to,"he said, lamely. "I was only a correspondent. It waa like my cheek to interfere." , _ _ _ . . _ .

"I—l'm glad I interfered with that engine," said the girl. "I really cannot get this glove on by myself." "And you carried Lieutenant Featherstone's body out of the thick of th light, with Boer sharpshooters pinging at you all the time?" said the mother._
"Please don't talk about it," pleaded Home. "I was In a terrible funk."
The girl made a little movement e!! her wrist just as Home had nearly.sueeeeded in buttoning her •glove. He had to begin all over again. Somehow, his hand shook.
"Have 1 hurt you ?" she a,Ancl.

"Yes—you're hurting Me now," stammered Hoe. "That is—l mean—" He did not know what he meant. Apparently the girl did, for a still lovelier calour stole into her cheeks. "Come in when you have rested," she said;" and mother and daughter left him.
Tioma"fell into a i•Py^rie. "What's my pulse going like this for?" he murmured. "Dashen silly nonsense I It's—it's only grz4itode to her for looking so beautiful."

A suddsn chill ran through him. Another girl =this dine a dark one—stood regarding him from the doorway of the ballroom. She was evidently a Russian, tall, sallow, black-eyed, with 'that inscrutable look which comes froth dwelling on snowy steppes. And there was a sneer upon her handsome lips. "Monsieur is seeing Paradise with the aid of his countrywoman ? " she asked. Home's shoulder twitched. With a rustle of black and amber draperies, she floated towards him. _ .
"Oh, you don't knaiv me! You don't know me! And yet I also, saved your life." Home was 13olitely incredulous. "Pardon me, but we have never met before." _
"Oh, yes, we have, Mr. Home. You were in St. Petersburg when there was a plot to blow up the Czar." _
"The Czar is always being blown up," said Home, in tired tones: "He would have died had it not been for you."
"Why, what had I to do..with it?" The girl.sat down on the sofa beside him. "I was going to throw the bomb when I caught sight of you close to the Czar' cCentourale," she said composedly.
'iWell ?-" ."You were so handsome that I—l didn't throw." TO
"What hadl to clo with it?" "It was an unusually powerful bomb. would have b2en shattered into little pieces." "I am very much indebted to you for your fc;.- bearance."

"You blight to , be," she cried, passionately.- ' I know you were coining here and—and awaited your arrival." "Why ? " "Why? Oh, mom DiNc You ask me .why? Why does a woman follow a man to the ends of the earth ?" _ _ . _

The overwhelmed 'Home murmured ' that he supposed it woman followed it man to the ends cf the earth because she ought not to. The woman gazed at him with gathering fury. • ' "Bah! I ought to have blown you to pieces, you cold, insensible Englishman." "It might, perhaps, have saved a certain amount of trouble," acidly agreed Home. "I see how it is. Now that I have made myself known to you--" "Pardon me, you haven't." "Oh, .1 forgot." She looked .round and whispered: "I am Vera Gotschakoff. Now do you know me?" Home rose frigidly. "You should never allow personal considerations to interfere with your work. Didn't you get into trouble for not throwing that bomb ? ' "Oh, yes, it knife thrust in the Bide. from one of'our committee. He's in Siberia now, poor fellow" '

The young Englishwoman floated past the open do-or, steered by a dexterous middy, who seemed to have his heart in his work. Home, clad in rough tweeds, sighed. suppose I am too late," said Vera Gotseha- koff. "The steam-engine girl Was before me— you can't forget that ? There is another thing you might also remember."
"Ye-:es ? " "I still have that. bomb."
,"Oh, indeed! I shoUld chunk it . into the bay If I were you." "But yOu are not me—stupid Englishman that ydu are !" "COmeborno It w an-fully kind of you not to throw that bomb. Let us be friends." A

. "Yes," she said, apparently softening. "Let ,us be frier.ds. Only, remember that come first. If you forget that„something unpleasant will happen. Some—thing un --if plea sant! Please take me into the ballroom." ."What! Like this ?"

"I would go with you in anything, anywhere." Home had to talic'her into Ole ballroom. Ono side of it was All window,- and the population of St. Pruden gatheled there, noses glued to the glass. He felt klorry that- they should look on while others danced, and _told- -Mario, the waitress,lo take them out a couple of gallons of cider: Every time he gazed at the blue-eyed girl he felt that Vera .Gotschakoff watched him. Collecting his energies at last, he went up to Miss Patton and begged for a dance. "My things haven't come on here yet," he said. "Can you dance with a bear in tweeds ?" llut his strained arm could not hold her sprained wrist. "Let us go into the other room and talk," he suggested, after a few turns. "I have been wanting to thank you properly ever since you came in." ttlVhat for ? " "Saving my life." "Was that so much to you?" "Not until you saved it."
They went Into the other room, Home feeling that the bomb might /come whirling after them at any moment. • .

In a week, Home-and the blue-eyed girl were engaged. How it had come about so rapidly neither of them- knew, naless it was that the consciousness of peril stimulated Home to un- usual effort. Ho might be wanted at the other end of the earth at any moment. On the other hand, Miss Patton explained that, as she had nearly dislocated M. Homo's arm, and he had been the Cause of spraining her (Wrist, they had Joined forces as a means of self-preservation. Vera Gotschakoff had apparently forgotten her threats. She would, however, lean on her elbow at dijettner, and, sadly regarding Homo from the depths of her sombro eyes, ask in audible tones whether Miss-Vatton really understood him. After a time, Miss Patton began to be annoyed. "Do you think I understand You ? " she asked Home sne evening. "Quite as much as is good for me.' "And you belong to me ? "- "Indubitably." - "Then what does that woman mean ay daring to make eyes at you all tho time? Is she mad ? " "Yes—a bit. Besides, she's a Nihilist." "Oh—h!" "She'd think nothing of blowing us up." Miss Patton laughed. "She's done that already." Home was vaguely uneasy. "Don't irritate her," he implored. :You never know what a fanatic like that may do. She's got a bomb in her room, and threatens to throw it at us if the engagenient is not broken off." "It strikes me," said ' Miss Patton, "that mamma had 'better take us away. Then this mad woman won't have anyone to throw bombs at unless she goes back to St. Petersburg." t` St. Prudoe is an ideal spot for lovers." She looked at him with big, blue, serious eyes. "Don't I make any spot ideal/ whore I happen to be ?"
_ "Just What r was trying to put into words. Shows how well you understand
Vera Gotsehakoff came into the salon and glared at them. Had Home told Miss Patton about the bomb? _ _ _ _

"Keep her her for ten minutes," whispered Miss Patton, greatly to Home's surprise. Then she said Mond: "Yes, I shall bp waiting for you at the foot of the Calrairo des Marins at nine o'clock," and hurried away. Vera Gotsehakoff sneered. As she swayed, towards him, she reminded Home of a panther about to spring. "It is time," she said, "that we had an explanation." Home brought her a chair. Mindful of Miss Patton's injunction, he smiled pleasantly. "Anything I can do " .

‘riaCou iliust break off your engagement with that chit of a girl or I will kill you both." "I don't think I'd do that if I were you., You might get into trouble. , We've neither of us done you any harm." . "Nei—,---7 Oh, you Make me mad! You 'have blasted nV. career--"'
"Of usefulness as a Nihilist ? " "She has dared to make love to you under my
eyes." "No, you're mistaken there. Honestly, rya done all the love-making." , "Bah! You call that love-making?"

"What do you call it?" • "I call it disgusting." "Sort Of disgust I've been hopmg to experience all my life. Now., look here, Miss Clotschakoff, I'm awfully obliged to you for not blowing me up in St. Petersburg, and all that; but why can't you let me be happy in my own way?" "Ha, you say that! But I will blow you up now. I will kill you." ,"You can if you like. It isn't consistent." "What isn't? What do, I care for con- sistency ?" "Well, you say ypu love me, and you spared inc in St. Potersburt. What's the use of sparing me in St. Petershurr and hlowirc, um up here 2 " ••Then you were free to loVe me. Now you despise me." "No, no, I don't. /i'o right-minded man despises a woman who really loves him," "I could give you a career,"

”Thank you; I don't want one. lam content to be loved." "Loved! By an sEnglish inees.' Bah! She won't love you as I do. , "I hope not: Can't. You see that you are altogether wasting yourself on me ?' I'm not worthy of so much affection. Why don't you go back to Russia, and chuck up Nihilism and settle down? ,You've had your little fling." - PI "I have had my little fling, you say? yart 'do not know. Wait and see. In an hour:, perhaps two hours, perhaps later, you will see.' *Miss Patton put her head in at the door. "Mamma has a headache and we dine in our own rooms. Meet me at the Calvliire des .Marins nine o'clock. I'm just going to dress." • Home did not understand -what It all meant. The Calvaire des Marina was a lonely cross on the. ,top of a mound overlooking the bay: He turned to leave the room. 'Vera Gotschakoff looked at him curiously. Her lips were set tight, the pupils of her yos contracted into vicious Slits: You won't give her up ? " "Of course I won't." Home MaaC another. attempt. "My dear girl, do forget this folly. div.p: TE.ADINa IN RUISAN SHIN.

As skin grafting on a large scale corder, :Li, more dxtensi re use in surgery, it becomc§ more difficult to procure the best material for the purpose. The difficulty has recently been met in America by treating the skin as an article of commerce, and buying the amount required. Five dollars (about £1 sterling) was the price paid by a doctor for 'sufficient skin to ,put on .the limb' of a little boy Who had been badly scalded.

div.head: DISEAStID GLASS.
div.p: A DISEAStID GLASS.

The authorities of the • Royal Museum at Dresden have .discovered a glass vase in - one of their show-cascs; dating from the eigh- teenth century, • which shows every. Sign of suffering from a wasting disease, and not only is it wasting away, but the authorities declare it has infected. the • other gla3 vessels in ' its immediate • neighbourhood. The vase has been carefully examined by experts and various- Medicines, •externally applied, have been prescribed to stay the progress .pf the malady, . but all to no pttrpoSe.

div.head: KETTLES THAT SING.
div.p: KETTLES THAT SING.

The Japanese, who know so well bow to add little unexpected attractions to every-day life, manufacture, in a great variety of forms, iron teakettles which break into song when the water boils. The song may not be a very perfect melody, bilt it is perhaps as agreeable as the notes produced by some of the insects which the Japanese also treasure for their music. ' The harmonious sounds of the tea- kettles are produced by steam bubble:4 escap- ing from beneath. thin sheets of iron fastened close tog2ther nearly at the bottom of the kettles. These singing kettles have been used for many centuries.

div.head: LIVING ON STILTS.
div.p: LIVING ON STILTS.

The people live .on. sixteen-foot stilts in the remarkable turpentine-growing - country of France. They don these stilts after break- fast. They do not remove them again till it is time for bed. There are two reasons for the wearing of' these stilts. One is the tur- pentine gathering. The other is the herding of the great flocks. The turpentine cornea from the maritime pine. The tree is tapped, a shingle is inserted, and from the shingle is hung a tiny bucket; into which the turpmitine drips. Young pine trees are= tapped low, but with each yearti3 pass-age the incision is made higher up; so that it is not long before. *most of the trees are tapped twenty or thiriy.feet from the groUnd. Hence the liege -stilts of the Workmen.. On these stilts they traverse the flat country, covering five to irix yards with one stride. •

div.head: LAXGEST WINE HOLDER.
div.p: LAXGEST WINE HOLDER.

What is probably the largest receptacle for wine in the world is a tank, cut out of solid rock, capable of holding half-a-million gal. ions. It is situated in the Italian-Swiss Colony of Asti in Southern California. When the structure was completed a festive gather- ing was held inside, and a hundred couples found ample space for dancing. .

div.head: CRADLE OF CORNISH CHRISTIANITY.
div.p: CRADLE OF CORNISH CHRISTIANITY.

In the obscure Cornish village of Ferran- zabuloe lying almost amidst the sandhilis that stretch from Perranporth to Newqua,y, there may be -seen the now fast disappearing remains of the earliest Christian ,Church in• England. It is known as St Pin's Ora- tory, and. was built somevlthere at the close of the Sth century, A.D. At an early date, which cannot be fixed with any degree of certainty, violent . sandstorms swept over the church and buried it. In 1835 a violent storm swept a portion of the sand away and uncovered a corner of the Oratory. Interest Was then taken in preserving the remains, but the wind and rain -have nearly demolished the church, ad what was, the cradle of Cornish. Christianity is in danger of becoming a rub- bish heap.

div.head: TITE EARTH-EATING HABIT.
div.p: TITE EARTH-EATING HABIT.

An investigation of geophagy, or the earth. eating habit, has shown that its excuses in- clude a liking for the odour ad taste of the variety of clay - eaten, an unnatural craving duo to disease, an attempt to satisfy hunger, the force of example, and supposed medicinal virtrr-s. The habit seems to exist all over the worn Fine clay, or stone butter, is eaten on bread in Germany, and earth is baked in bread in Sweden and the Kola peninsula; and is found in the markets of par_ts of Italy. The Percians ,use it in sweetmeats; the Nubians as medicine. ;Gray shale is much: eaten in Northern India. • Another great delicacy is soil containing white ants and their nests.

div.head: CABIN OF BONES.
div.p: CABIN OF BONES.

The queerest house in the world is pro- bably the famous Bone Cabin in WYomingb near the Medicine Bow river. This cabin'. foundations are built of fossil bones. Bones of dinosaurs—jaws of the'. diplodocus, teeth Of the brontosaurus, knuckles of the ichthyosau- rus, vertebrae of the eamarasaurus, Chunks of the baros aunts, the cetiasaurus, the brachipsaurus, the stegiosaurus, the ornitho- lestes, or hire- catching dinosaur all entered into this wonderful cabin's foundations. This hut was built by a Mexican sheepherder, who had kap- pened by chance on the grandest extinct animal bed in the world. This was a plot about fifty yards square, wherein lay in rich profusion the bones of all the animals of the Reptilian Age. The place was evidently once a river bar, and the dead bodies that 'floated down the stream were arrested to lie there for hundreds of thousands of years.

div.head: 210)3BY.HORIIE IN A PULPIT.
div.p: 210)3BY.HORIIE IN A PULPIT.

IA curiosity Which never fails to excite the interest of all visitors to the old parish ! church of Berkswell, near Coventry, is a very high saddle shaped tcol, known as the pul- pit hobby-horse, ,to be seen in the vestry. It ' seems that .about the year 1750 the rector of Berkswell was very fond of riding, and it is said that he was far more at home in the saddle than he was in the pulpit. So he had , a stool made with the seat padded and ' shaped like a saddle, which could. be plaCed in the pulpit before lie ascended the steps, and on which he could sit whilst delivering his sermon, instead of standing. By this , means he hoped to infuse more 'life and spirit into his sermon.

JOHN CHINAMAN'S RECEIPT. / Every three years all Chinamen living in Siam have to pay a mien poll-tax. When this has been paid the collector ties a string , round the man's left wrist and fastens the knot with a special official seal. The curious bracelet thus formed constitutes John China- • man's receipt, and- he must wear it for a • period of at least one month after paying. If , during that time he is caught without it ho must pay over again. It is very amusing to r watch the revenue officers and police round- ing up the Celestials at tax-time and inspect- ing their arms. It is said that many hurt- dreds of Chinamen evade payment alto- gether by wearing string with counterfeit seals.

div.head: COTTAGE HOMES.
div.p: THE COTTAGE HOMES.

At a meeting of the Padgate Cottage Homes Com- mittee the Superintendent reported that the Cheshire Lines Engineers Cricket Club gave their annual treat to the boys on July 11th, that the bcys' railway fares were paid and each boy received a prize or a present. A great number of presents, nuts, sweets, &c. were sent for the girls. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Cricket Club for their generosity. A letter was read from the Rev. Father Allen resigning his appointment as Roman Catholic instructor. The resignation was accepted and it was decided that the Right Rev. Dr. Whiteside, Bishop of Liverpool, be asked to nominate a successor. It was resolved that the children be taken for a trip to New Brighton on Tuesday of next week. The minutes were approved. itoi; SFI COMMITTEE.

Mr. 13rsT seconded. Mr. MATnER,bo had given notice of motion that the relief committee meetings be held at 9 instead of 9.30, said that since the last meeting a great Fbange had come over the scene. A fortnight ago there were 120 or 130 cases, but to-day thsre were only about CO. He did not think any ulteration Was necessary, under tha circumstances.

The Rev. Father RYAN said that there were fewer eases that etty but he believed the decrease would be only temporary. During the prat few weeks no fewer than 120 or 140 hands had been stopped at one works in Mr. Garnett's district. At the last meeting one of the Guardians Fn id the relief committee, against the advice of the relieving officer, gave relief to an able- bodied man who refused to support his wife when the was ill. To his (Father Ryan's) recollection no such case came before them, lie was strongly in favour of altering the time of the Board meeting as at present it was impossible to give sufficient time to the business. Miss BROADBENT said tbe administration of out- relief was about the most important work the Guardians did. The point she wished to emphasise was that the out-relief in the Warrington district had pone up by ZiO since the reorganization of the committee. . . . . . .

On Mr. ilnootis's resolution being put to the meet- ing eight voted for it and eight against. The CHAIRMAV said it was absolutely immaterial to him she the meetings were held. He could be there at six in the morning if they wished. Mr. FORSHAW : You are one of the leisured clasies. (Lsugbter.) The CHAIRMAN abstained from voting and Mr. Mather withdrew his resolution,with the result that the old arrangement obtains. It is, however, open to the Relief Committees to make any suggestion as to their hour of meeting.

div.head: – THE REPAYMENT OF RELIEF.
div.p: - THE REPAYMENT OF RELIEF.

In accordance with instructions given at the last meeting the CLERK submitted the following return showing the amounts received by the collector in respect of in-maintervince.out-relief,and lunatics during the nixteen weeks ended 18th July, 1908 :—ln-maintec- army, £99 68. id.; out-relief, £74 lb. Id.; lunatics, £lO7 Os. ed. ; total, £341 Is. lie explained that during that period only two orders of repayment had been made in Mr. Garnett's district, and that showed the cases bad been very poot itkdeed, Mr. BILLINGE : Does it not mean that the house test has been rigidly applied in tbis district ? Mr. MATITER : No, it cannot mean that, because the out-relief has gone up. The CHAIRM AN : SO far as I understand, the poverty of the people accounts for it. Mr. FURNESS said the return appeared to be rather inadequate, for he thought it should include the amounts due, the sums collected, and the extent of the ariears in each district. The CLERK promised to prepare a full return for the next meeting.

INCREAEE OE' RELTE.F. The CLERK said be hid received trom the Local, Government Board a very important return showing the amounts expended by Boards of Guardians for poor relief during the half-year ending Lady Day 1907 and a similar statement for the half-year ending Michaelmas 1907. The statements were given under three hvids— (l) in-maintentince, (2) maintenance of paupers in establishments not provided by Poor Law authorities, (3) outdoor relief. The Warrington Union during that period showed an increase of 10 per cent, and there was only one other Union in the North-Western - district and seventeen in the Kingdom which showed an increase to that extent. It was a most important return and he suggested that each Guardian be supplied with a copy. Mr. Billinge asked if the increased expenditure was not largely accounted for by sending children to lust itutions. The CLERK: T hardly think that explains it because if wq. did not send them to homes we should have to pay for them. It was agreed that each Gmirdian should be furnished with a copy of the rettun.

THE C;t7ARDIANS'- PRIVATE It 4NKING ACCOUNT. The CLERK reed a letter from the Local Government Board asking for the Guardians' observations on an extraot from the District Auditor's report, it? which he called attention to a private banking account of the Guardians. . . .

It wes decided that the letter be referred to the Finance and General Purposes Committee. The CLIRK said he had prepared a return of the receipts and expenditure under the private account. It was proposed that this matter should also be referred to the Finance and General Purposes Committee which consists of the whole Board. Mr. W. C. Brworts : I don't think we should hoodwink this any longer. 'tans been hoodwinked long enough, and I move that it be thrashed out by the Board, Mrs. Wir.KissoN seconded.'

Mr. FORSRAW : We ought to discuss the matter publicly. Mr. Brrxixor. : It is not Union business. It is simply a private account. It does not receive anything from the ratepayers. Mr. W. C. BROOKS It is ratepayers' money. Mr. FORSHA w: There should be no private accounts in public matters. Mr. Lim. said many members,including himself, were quite ignorant as to the private account and he objected to the matter being disct ssed publicly. Mr. FURNESS objected to the matter ,being publicly discussed now because they did kot know exactly what they were discussing. Iles moved that the Clerk send copy of tho return to every Guardian and that the Finance and General Purposes Committee should then discuss the matter. Mr. DENT seconded and this was agreed to.

FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
GLORIOUS WEATHER AND KEEN CONTESTS.

The tw.enty.third annual spmts of ths Warrington Football Club which took place on the Wildersoool enclosure on Bank Holiday fully maintained the high reputation which the meeting has rong held in the district A beautifully fine afternoon, a large attend- ance, and keen racing combined to make the affair a success -a fact upon which the promoters are entitled to . congratulate themselves. There was nothing lacking to ensure an interesting afternoon for the spectators and so largo were the entries that it took four and a half hours to get through the nineteen events. The contests generally were tell fought and some exciting finishes were witnessed, particularly in the bicycle handicaps. The arrangements were all that could be desired, and mention must be made of the excellent work of the officialQ, who were as follows : —Clerk of the Course, Mr. T. Bowers ; starter, Mr. T. Wainwright ; judges, Messrs. T. Locker, E. Picka- -1 Vance (N.C.U.) and A. Booth (N.C.U.) ; time-keeper Mr. J. E. Warren; committee, Messrs. W. Hewitt, W, Chalmers, F. T. Barber, W. Nevins, J. Dutton, F. Heesom, W. Hill, I. Hackett, F. Turner, E. Gilbert, J. W. Evans. A. Jones, J. Winstanley and Henry Hope ; handicapper, Mr. IT. N. Ellis ; hon. treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton ; hon. cemetery, 'Mr. H. Ashton ; official representative N.CU, Mi. W. Taylor, Se. Helens. The Borough Band was in attendance and enlivened the proceedings xvith some capital selections. I

div.head: "I HAVE DONE IT."
div.p: "I HAVE DONE IT."

A man named Patrick Tyrol, a labourer, is at present an inmate of the Widnes AcCideut Hospital suffering from oxalic poisoning. On Wednesday evening while in the bar of the Moss Bank Hotel he was seen to drink something from a bottle, and he then said, "I have done it." lie was given as emetic by a chernist at Sulltvams works, nud afterwards attended by Dr. Caughey, His condition is not considered dangerous.

Rome, it appears, still con- THE PAPAL tinues to dream of the con- CHURCH AND version of England. Indeed, THE ENGLISH the present idea seems to PEOPLE. be that the work will be carried out in the lifetime of one man who is already fairly well advanced in years. Father VAUGHAN is to be the new St. Augustine, and we infer from the rather vague telegram cf a newspaper correspondent in Rome that he has gone to a Mission House in Washing- ton to prepare himself for his work,the said Mission House having been established with the view to the conversion of the English-speaking peoples to Roman Catholicism. Cardinal MERRY DEL VAL, who was himself educated in England, and who -at Rome seems to be more powerful than the Purr, says that Father VAUGHAN has " all the qualities that are most apt to secure the best results, and that to him has fallen the providential role of caerying to ultimate success the projects of his uncle, the late Cardinal." We know Father VAUGHAN as a successful and rather sensational preacher ; but we should not have suspected him of these large designs. Probably he attracts to any place in which he may preach many hearers who art% not of the Roman Catholic communion. Smart society probably enjoys the denunciation of its sins from the pulpit; but we doubt whether it is in process of coni,ersion to any Church what- ever, unless it is a Church into which it can carry its sins with it.

Twenty-five to thirty years ago such an announcement as that fresh steps were to be taken to convert England to the Rornish Church would have been the occasion of a reat deal of excite- ment and agitation. Thdre would have been 3turphy riots and what not. But hardly a single pulse will be quickened by the present news from Rome. Probably not even the Konsitites will be moved to additional activity ; for the Kensitites see one thing clearly enough, which is that if England is converted to Rome, an event of which there is not the least likelihood, the work will be done by %ea in the Church of England much more than by the missions of the Church of Rome. Nothing has happened since Lord JOHN' nossinn wrote up "No Popery," and then ran away to justify the fears then entertainel as to the results of establishing a R nnan hierarchy in Engfind. There have been great men at the head of the 'English movement, fiery missioners like Cardinal WISEMAN, impassioned writers and preachers like ,Cardinal NEweLLN, ecclesiastical statesmen and social reformers like Cardinal MaN2inco ; but

nothing eurprising has happened. We should be- surprised to to hear that the adherents to Roman Catholicism in this country have increased in number -much out of proportion to population. We have had many dotts of revivals, but there has been no memorable Catholic revival. Perhaps we may expect an attempt at something of the sort - when Father VON—who, by the way,"does not strike us by .any personal resemblance to PETER the Ilnantr —returas from Washington. There is profound truth in the old saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church. It is a persecuted firm of religion which makes most headway. Perfect tolerance is 4pt to dis- courage all forms of religious excitability, from that of the Cardinal to that of the street preacher; "We will fight hostile tariffs by free imports,' said Sir ROBERT PEEL on a memorable occasion' Roman Catholic efforts to convert England have been defetted by tolerance. Roman Catholicism has had a free 8.,311 for many years past. Nohody has attempted to oppress it. Outside of its own ranks nobody takes a great deal of notice of it. At Westminster it has built th) largest cathedral that has .been erected since the Middle Ages; but there was no public excitement on the subject, Hardly anybody seemed to think it mattered, except those v,ho were already members of the Roman Catholic Church. ,What is felt nowadays, in fact, is that the nal danger is in the Church of England, where there is much real and passionate desire to procure the general adoption cf beliefs and practices which are not distinguishable from those of the Church of Rome. A Roman Catholic con- version of E3glancl, if it were possible, would be all the more improbable because in this country Roman Catholicism does not touch the large masses of the people at any perceptible point. It is for the most part out of sympathy with them politically. It is more of the classes than the masses, and we venture to think that, so far from converting England in his lifetime, FATTIER VAUGILN will lay down his work—many years from now, we trust—in much the same condltion as that in which he takes it up.

If no one else is alive to the fact we suppose the old folks will be well aware that Old-Age Pensions are within a few months of being an accomplished fact. The Bill has received the Royal assent, and Mr. John Burns, the President of the Local Government Board, is already hustling the Town and Urban Councils to set about the formation of pension committees. One of the dreams of years will soon be realised, and the old people saved from penury by a beneficent State. The pension officers are to he appointed by the Treasury, and they will report to the local com- mittees on esch_elaim. The Committees will have the consideration of all claims, and may be person- ally appealed to by applicants: Forms for per,sion claims are expected to be available at post offices on October let. The Warrington Town Council will consider the formation of a Pension Committee on Tuesday next.

The annual meeting of the THE Sine CANAL. Manchester Ship canal Company on Thursday was somewhat depressing. Shareholders in the com- pany may not feat much concerifed at the slump in trade on the Canal, because they have never received any dividends in the whole fourteen years; that the great conearn has been working. What does riot exist cannot be diminished, and as the. e - original subscribers have also given up hope of, , receiving any interest on their money, the regretful , accents of Mr. Bythell, the chairman of the Cam- ' ), pany, would not touch them to the quick. It ise is not to be wondered at that, with the-, universal depression in trade, the Gen AI CAI- : pany's returns should show a falling awary. But the decrease in receipts is not ''-' by any means paralysing, amounting 119 it does to only £11,503 for the twelve months. The worse features are that the slump in trade has occurred almost wholly within the, past half-year, and that' the prospects for the ensuing three months are not bright. We are passing through a lean time, and i the reaction after nine years of booming trade is le not phenomenal though it may be disturbing. The .: Canal Company has contrived to make a working ' profit of £103,027, the decrease beieg 1/10,698, while expenditure has also decreased, so that the position of affairs is not without its encouraging side. In fact, Mr. Bythell, after painting the, --: ' picture in gloomy tones, concluded by expressing the confident opiiiion that the time when the shareholders may expect some remuneration is approaching. We suppose it is—in company with I the millennium. The poor dog is grateful:, Ifor the dryest bone, however, and we hope the ere shareholders wilt he able within measurable 1 time to acclaim Mr. Bethell a prophet. Mean- - i Iwhile, it seems to us that in addition to the establishment of a spot cotton market in Mani cheater, there is a great want of industriae .4 ' development along the banks of the waterway ee For instance, Warrington cannot boast of contri- buting very largely to the carrying trade of the .-- canal, though there are evidences of enterprise. The past fourteen years should have seen a much more rapid developmeet of manufactures along the waterway. When the vessels pass between lines of wharves and warehouses—and ' not wheat- fields—then will be the tina3 to talk of and expect divideeds. .

After the gloomy prognosti• FARR'S Runt. cations which have filled the air of rate, it was refreshing to hear the optimistic tone characterising Mr. Cecil F. Parr's speech at the half-yearly meeting of Parr's Bank, Ltd., at Warrington on Thursday. Speaking in such an influential position as that of chairman of an important concern like Parr's Bank, Mr. Parr's words always carry considerable weight. His speeches do not consist of dry details of matters solely concerning the shareholders, for Mr. Parr takes a broad outlook and touches upon questions which are agitating the - financial world and the public generally. On Thursday his prin- cipal topic was the state of trade and he still holds to the view that the present state of affiirs is a set back from the previous unprecedented expansion rather than the beginning of a whole- sale and continued depression. He laid emphasis upon the feet that our exports for the five months ending June last, which amounted co £149,000,009, were only a decraase of 7 per cent, on the first five months of the previous re:ord year, and that - they would, in fact, have constituted a record had they not been ec!ipsed by the figures for 1907. 'Applying another tee, the bankruptcies and liquidations during the extraordinarily prosperous year ending June 1907 totalled 9,716 a,nd yet in the following year, when things wore supposed to be going from bad to worse, the number was only 95774—an increase of 64. , Mr. P.irr therefore feels justified in concluding that in some parts the stories of depression may have been exagerated and he ii hopeful that when the large stocks which have been left over from the " piping tidies" of the early months of last year have been worked off, an iinpreveruent in trade may ba looked for. Warriogtora in common with other industrial centres, will heartily re-echo the senti- ment. As usual Mr. Parr was able to submit a rosy statement of the bank's position and prospects, and, viewed from all standpoints, the balance sheet afforded indisputable evidence of the bank's stability and prosperity.

Pt'obably everyone has MR. H. G. WELLs realised by this time that AND in Mr. 11. G. Wells this Soormsar. country has produced an original thinker ' an d dreamer on social problems. He imagines ilirn• self to, be a Socialist, but ho frankly cuts him- self off from the ordinary Socialist because ho declares no war upon the capitalist and landlord classes. He admits that " Socialism mast, lovingly but ,resolutely, use I law, use force to dispossess the owners of socially disadvantageous wealth, as one takes a wrongfully acquired toy from a spoilt and ob,iticate child," so that when it cornea to the, point Mr. Wolfs would be in the same boat with the moat \revolu- tionary Marxist. Still he differs from them in laying less stress upon political programmes, being in fact oppossol to direct political action at all. But the peculiarity of his teaching is that it contains -a 'message to the individual. ' Instead of denouncing at the street corner the wealthy who give nothing to the world in return for the material end educational blessings with which. by an accident of birth they, are endowed, Mr. Wells directs his' message to the wealthy themselves, bids them to be ashamed of 3 useless life of mere pleasure, and preachcS. a semi- ToLstoyar, doctrine of self-denial and social service. His difference from Tolstoy is that the latter wishes to destroy organised human society, his ideal being philosophical Anarchism, while Mr. Wells calls upon each one, in his capacity as a worker iu some department—as a lawyer, a writer, an organiser of industry, or what not—to modifY society so far as he can in the direction of social democracy. An interesting line of argument, one must admit.

It is announced that there is to, be an Inteinaticnal Amity Conference at Rome in October. Tha Inter Parliamentary Peace Conference' which has found its origin in the International Arbitration Leagnn established by the late Sir Randal Cromer, meets in Berlin in September. Some people will regret that these organisations are rising up and meeting at different times, without the advantage of the unity of movement which is so desirable. But is it not 'quite possible that each has ti leavening influence which coulknot be gained at this stage if all were working together? The most encouraging fact about the political outlook jiln now is that we are stretching hands across national barriers. The scientific societies are becoming international; the trade union bodies are making another network; then different religious societien find common bonds of sympathy. Yet another cause of linking up is the way in which the peoele of various countries are making financial investments in other countries. ' The British capitalist has his money in Germany, Russia, 03 France—ehe more money he has there the less he is likely to desire anything but peace. ' The influence of French money in Russia has had a lot to do with curbing autocratic sentiment there, much more than appears on the surface. The sooner that the arbitrary lines of nationality nre broken down the better it will be for the world, provided only that constitutional rules of govern- ment and of administration obtain. Even the Sick Man of Turkey seems now to be resigned to establishing a Constitution which shall be some- thing more than an empty name.

Slams occupies a romantic situation on the verge of -the cliffs. This place was visited by Dr. Johnson and 'Boswell during their tour in Scotland, when they dined, supped, and slept at the Castle, and they devoted the afternoon of the day to an excursion to the famous Bailers of Buchan, the groat sight of the dist' ict.
