Mr. H. G. Wells has an article in the " Contem- Nrary Review" on" My Socialism " in which he Bays: I disavow the Socialism of revolt. There is a I°rEn of Socialism based upon the economic generaliza- tions of Marx, an economic, fatalistic Socialism that I hold to be rather wrong in its vision of facts, rather more distinctly wrong in its theory, and altogether "wrong and hopeless in its spirit. It preaches aS inevitable, a concentration of property in the hands of a limited number of property owners, and the ZPropriation of the great proletarian mass of man- kind, a concentration which is, after all, no more than a tendency conditional on changing and changeable c,onventions about property, and it finds its hope of a better future in the outcome of a class conflict between the expropriated many and the expropriat- ing few. Both sides are to be equally swayed by self- interest, but the toilers are to be .gregarious and mutually loyal in their self-interest—Heaven knows 'will, except that otheruise the Marxist dream will network

* * * The neatest practical example of the resnite of a Tariff that we have yet seen was given at the Inter- : national Free Trade Congress by Mr. Heringa, who / compared the cost of commodities in two places —the -• e, Ensched4, in Holland, under the all-but Free -trade system which the Dutch enjoy ; the other, . Grenau, which is five miles across the border in Germany, and comes under the Imperial Tariff t rerything in the German town is dearer by, roughly 'aPeaking, the amount of the teL It would be quite , useless t 3 tell an inhabitant of either place that taxes ' do not raise prices. They know otherwise, and act on their knowledge, like sensible people : Some 603 to 700 labourers go every day from . EesehelfS (Holland) to Gronan (Germany) and come back in the evenin,, because the cost of living in .. their own country is much lotver. A whole village Of 4,000 inhabitants has grown up at Glanerburg, in —Holland, near the German frontier ; Furl on Dutch groand the German marmfacturers build houses for a whole,oolony of their workmen, because ,the can live more cheaply and better in the foreign country. S it is in Germany, so it would be here if we were oolish enough to impose the same conditions. •Taxes • oa the necessaries of life hive, of coarse, their inevit- able effect of raising the cost of living. ~„. acr onee in a way the weather during the whole of •, :, . the groat August holidays has been absolutely porfect. .; cell day of brilliant sunshine has teen followed by . • night almost more beautiful, with starry skies and ~. rescent moon ; and perhaps most beautiful of all have , .•en the early mornings, wh m the air was as crystal- „ ear as it is round Swiss peaks at sundae, and when .he trees especially; with the foliage perfectly still, ▪ area wondrous sight to see. It has been hot, as it • nni,l be, in August, but never sultry, and one 131 easing effect of this state of things was that far fOwer fathers and mothers, whose Bank Holiday con- ''Sts of taking a band ~of youngsters for a picnic .to ' ' !"-le heath or sylvan glade, looked worn out and s "nnry on the way home. They went out giggling and 'chattering with bags and bundles -of food ; they - Patronisedathe ginger-beer seller and the ice-cream !?lan right royally, and they came home singing and )Vial, with shelves of bracken already half-dead, and eri ~ th a harvest of blackberries which were none the 'es% precious because they were as green as grass and na hard as steaes. * * * An interesting letter in the ', Westminster t‘razette " discusses the origin of the description of c,bo 'nine of diamonds" card as "the curse of oeotland." The phrase ie often used to-day in card -13 lay and probably few people know the meaning of it. .111 the course of his letter, Mr. W. P. Courtney says: a forgotten volume on the obsolete game of whist 1 which I published fourteen years ago I cited seven different reasons, most of them connected with the unfortunate House of Stuart, which had been given 1 ab ,) out 1-0 years since for the name popularly attached t° this card. I added that the most frequent exclaim- ; tfon—making eight in all—is that the Duke of Linaberland used the back of that card for his order 1 or the massacre of the prisoners after Culloden, but that there isaibundant evidence that the card had been SO called long before that date. A writer in " Notes . and Queries" its May, 1893, while allowing this, naaintained that the Duke did write the order on , its ba-el and that the identical card was preserved at Slates Castle. The value of this statement was , destroyed by a subsequent communication in the same ' Paper in January 1894, stating on the authority of , Captain Webbe, who had married the sister of the Earl of Erroll, that the only card preserved in the castle among the Kilmarnock papers was the eight of diamonds, with a note on the back sent by the Duke - of Hamilton to the Countess di Yarmouth, which i1:01313r expresses regret at his not having been able , to call upon her." . div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.

[Facim OUR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.] When Parliament adjourned last Saturday, it left over for the autumn sitting a large quantity of serious work. But it completed achievements may be regarded with no little satisfaction. In the Old Age Pensions Bill and the Irish Universities Bill, which have received the Royal assent and passed into law, the Liberal Government has placed on the statute book two measures of the first impoita'nce. It is, of course the foundation, and not the finished edifice, of a system of Old Age Pensions that the new Act has constructed. Only an iavincible prejudice could fail to recognise the wise statesmanship of Mr. Asquith's decision that Old Age Pensions ought to be inaugurated in a plan characterised by simplicity in its working and moderation in its expendituie. The Irish Universities Bill was a great triumph for Mr. Birrell. Although the Nonconformists were at first inclined to fear that it was weighted with a denomina- tional bias, the majority of them realised, in the end, that this was not so. A University Which supplies the needs of a population in which the Roman Catholic element enormously preponderates will naturally take its tone from the prevailing element. But that is a different matter. An undenominational constitution has been established, with every reasonable safeguard for its permanence and stability. Mr. Birrell has solved a problem which has baffled every statesman before him. Ile has removed a religious grievance and an intellectual disability from which Ireland had suffered so long, and this without creating any fresh grievance or disability.- TRE LORDS AND PENSIONS.

Seddon, XL. said there was the important question of the dock regulations, which were issued in 1901. It was gener- ally supposed that the regulations would come into operation in three years' time. - The particular regulations to which he was directing attention referred to the loading and unloading of ships, and stated dnctly the functions and duties of shipowners. The complaint was' that only ; two shipping firms in Liverpool had tried to carry out this regulation. The dock inspector reported on this I matter, but instead of anything being done the other ; shipowners used their influence to compel the two ' shipping companies using ladders to take them away, because the Home Office was not interested in carrying out these regulations. The inspectors were helpless. They reported and reported, and that was the end of their operation. He maintained that nothing would bring about a change unless the inspectors were sup- ported by the Home Office to prosecute the shipowners to carry out the regulations. Speaking the other day, Sir Walter Runciman said that I whenever a Government Introduced legislation into ' commercial affairs they always made a mess of it. If that was the general opinion of the shipowners of the country, he (Mr. Seddon) was not at all surprised they , had not carried out the regulations laid down by the Home Office. He had a list of accidents which bad taken place at the various docks in the country. The hon. member referred to the case of the Dublin steamer Kilkenny. Some time ago one of the dockers was 'engaged trimming coal on that vessel, the coal began to move, and, there being no means of egress, the man Iwas in danger of being smothered, when he was rescued by his mates. Mr. Gladstone.—Was that this year? Mr. Seddon said it was last year before the rpgula- tions came in force, but in the meantime no attempt had been made to secure greater safety for the dockers. He asked the right hon. gentleman, through his inspectors in Liverpool, and other ports, to get sufficient informa- tion to enable him to prosecute shipowners who were wilfully ignoring the regulations. If the right hon. gentleman was unable to take that course then let him call a conference of shipowners and dockers, or let him receive a deputation of dockers' representatives, and he

AN ECONOMIC,' NECESSITY. Mr. Asquith's speech at the Cobden Club dinner was a complete eiposition of the whole case for Free Trade. Apart frpm the international aspect, with its all-important bearing on the peace of the world, Mr. Asquith's masterly presentation was chiefly concen- trated on the economic necessity of Free Trade for a small country with a teeming population, and the stability assured to our national finance by a policy of no taxation except for revenue. Great Britain was absolutely driven to the adoption of Free Trade by the impossibility of producing here at borne, " even under the most insuperable tariff that Protectionist architecture could design," the requisite food for our people and the indispensable material for our industries. The necessity which broke clown the old tariffs between 1840 and 1840, " coerces us with an ever- increasing stringency to follow along the same paths." The rapid growth of our population has enormously increased our need for free imports of food. The rapid growth of our industries has enormously increased our need for free imports of raw material. To-day our net imports of raw wool, which fifty years ago were about 00 millions of pounds avoirdupois, average over 30 millions of pounds; our net imports of raw cotton have risen from S million cwt.to 16 million cwt. By the rolicy of free imports we are able not only to feed and find employment for our population, but to beat our protectionist competitors out of neutral markets,to over leap their tariff walls,and in may cases to undersell the protected manufacturer in his own market. FREE TRADE AND SOUND FINANCE. A sure test of fiscal policy is its effects upon National Finance. Mr. Asquith drew a forcible con- trast between Free Trade Britain and Protectionist countries in the use which they have made respectively of three years of abundant prosperity. Great Britain has remitted many millions of taxation and has largely • reduced the National Debt. What Protectionist country

div.p: has been able to offer any similar boon to its tax- payers? And the reason why a Free Trade country is able to show so much advantage over its Protec- tionist neighbours is, that whatever taxes we may impose, they will always yield the whole proceeds to the National Exchequer, and no part of them will be retained or diverted to serve the particular purposes of special or privileged interests.

Mr. Gladstone said the case of the Kilkenny, he gathered, arose last year, land the regulations affecting it did not come into operation until January last. There was, therefore, no question of any failure to enforce the regulations. Two prosecutions had taken place in Liverpool this year, and during the month of April the services of two inspectors were fully directed to the question of enforcing the regulations. Mr. Sexton, the docker's representative, had made certain allegations, and had been asked to supply particulars, but had not yet replied. When the information was received it would be closely investigated. Mr. Bell. house, the superintendent inspector for the division, would arrange to meet Mr. Sexton in Liyerpool on an early date in order to personally investigate the whole question of the enforcement of the regulations. The inspectors had found considerable difficulty owing to the lack of help on the part of the workmen concerned. There had been a noticeable falling off in the number of complaints received, indicating that a good deal was being done.
The Examiner, Saturday, August 8, 1908.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS MAN'S FREAK.

Charles Orr, a labourer living at Burtonhead Farm, appeared quite bewildered when charged at St. Helens on Tuesday with being drunk la possession of firearms. Police-Constables Lewis and Charlton said the man was shouting and going about Sutton Heath-road at a quarter-past two on Sunday morning. The officers were on special duty, watching gardens and farm pro- duce, and when spoken to Orr said he had come out with the gnu to protect the farm and gardens. He was ‘ drunk, and said, ' I have come out to shoot anybody I can see." He was in a state of drunkenness, and having a loaded double-barrelled gun in his possession, he was locked up. Fined 10s. and costs. MOTORISTS FINED AT PRESCOT. At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, a number of motor-car owners and drivers were summoned for exceeding the limit of twenty miles per hour. Mr. C. F. Boston, leather merchant, of Huyton, was fined 20s. I and costs for driving his car at a speed of 25 miles 1,275 yards per hour over a measured quarter . mile in Knowsley-lane, Knowsley, on the 24th ult. H. W. Poey, I chauffeur, King's Heath, it was alleged, drove his car over a measured quarter mile, at Barnhill, at the rate of thirty-six miles per hour, on the 22nd ult. He was fined £2 and costs. Thomas Owen,ohauffeur, Liverpool, was fined .£2 and costs; William Knighton, chauffeur, Birkdale 30s. and costs ; Alfred E. Baxter, of Preston Brook (two offences), £5 and costs in each; Thomas A. Higgins, chauffeur, Hartford, 20s. and costs; and Frederick Sutcliffe, waste merchant, Huddersfield; 20s. and costs. BRUTAL HUSBAND. William Langley, a collier, Claughton-street, was charged by the St. Helens police on Tuesday, with breach of the peace.—lnspector Goodall said that early on Sunday morning he and a constable were called to Langley's house, where his wife and children were in a state of terror. He had some of his wife's clothing on the fire and had his wife's and children's clothing laid out in rotation ready to burn them. They had trouble with the same man on Saturday, and so he was locked up.—Mrs. Langley came up and besought the magistrates to save her life by granting e, separation. Yon years her husband had beaten her and destroyed the things in the house. He had run after her with knives. During I the past few days she had had to sleep out, and practi- cally got no rest. He said that if he could see her body in the mortuary before he went to prison he would serve time with a good heart. He said that fourteen days in gaol would only be a rest from the coalpit.— Langley was ordered to find sureties or serve twenty- eight days, and the wife was granted a separation, with an order for 7s. a week. JACK ASHORE. LIVELY TIME FOR ST. HELENS POLICE. George Derbyshire, a St. Helens man who has for some time been a gunner 03 board H.k.S. London I was charged at St. Helens on Tuesday with disorderly conduct and assaulting three otscers.—The evidence was that about half-past seven on Monday night, Derbyshire was staggering abon t the streets andinsult- ing females. Police-constable 'Lloyd ordered him off, but being in plain clothes, the sailor, refused to believe that he was a policeman and struck him. Police- constable Britch went to his assistance, and was at once butted heavily in the stomach, and practically "knocked out." Sergeant Moffatt then came on the scene, and was also subjected to rough treatment. The sailor said they Nybuld have to have a bit of ,j u-jitsu.—Derhy- shire now said he was sorry that he assaulted 13ritch, because he knew him very well, bet he did not believe that the other man was a constable. He did not remem- ber seeing the sergeant. He had been home on four day's leave. He was fined .4:1 15s. altogether, aud costs in four eases.

div.head: TAXATION OF LAND VALUES. Meeting at Bridge Foot._
div.p: TAXATION OF LAND VALUES. Meeting at Bridge Foot._

On Monday evening, Mr. Witley from Huddersfield' I spoke at an open air meeting at Bridge Foot about the Taxation of Land Values. Mr. Withy Laid that Professor Thorold Rogers had proved that in the fifteenth century a common labourer would in an eight h,ours day earn £l4O (one hundred and fully pounds !) according to present day's working money. If we take into consideration that for every human being several horse powers in engines arc working, that untold inventions have increased the producing power of the man to a marvellous degree, we came to the conclusion that to-day even the poorest man ought to enjoy a, comfort in life ichicli is only the lot of the very well-to-do—not to say the rich man: What is the difference in the social poadi dons of tri-clay as compared with the fifteenth cc:eV:ley? In the fifteenth century the landlord had to pay all the taxes; the labourer practically none; to-day labour, trade and iedustry pay all the taxes, the landlord as landlord pays a paltry sum of £750,000 on an assessment of the year 1602, being -Is. in the £ tax on the even then grossly under-estimated value. Let us demand that this 4s. in the £ tax in land etlue4 be levied on the actual values of to-day and it 'would yield according to the Financial Reform Altnanack's estimate at least £40,000,000. ' Add to this £3,000,000 from repeal of the Doles Act, we could appertiop - £13,000,003 as under : (a) Payment of members and of election expenses, £1,000,000 ; (h) Repeal of breakfast table duties, £11,000,000 ; (c) Old-ago pensions ss. per week for every one over 60 years, £25,000,000; (d) 2d. off the income tax £5,000,000 ; present yield of land tax £750,000 ; total, £43,000,000. But the effect would not end with this. Tnere are 12,000,000 acres of good cultivable land capable of sdpporting a family to every five or ten acres held idle for deer forest, game preserves ace while millions of acres more are only half used, 4 labour starved." Wer the Laud Tax of Is. in the £ levied on the full yearly value of all land, whether iu use or not,these 12,003,000 acres would soon bo put to nse. This moans that 1,200,000 families or 6,000,600 men, women and children would be drafted from the slums and the Milling districts into the country. There would be 1,200,000 families fewer oompeting for Wages in the towns and mining districts, therefore higher wages; 1,200,000 families fewer competing for houseroom, therefore more houseroom, for those left behind and lower house rants. But this is not all. The 1,200,000 families in the country would be producing wealth! On Lord Carrington's estate—Lord Carrington is a landlord who advocates the taxation of land values—the men make a clear average return of Hs. to 30s. a week, but averaging it only at 203. per week per family, those 1,200,000 families on the now derelict 12,000,000 acres i would afford a home market of upwards of £32,000,000 per annum for all-products of mine and factory, while the great increase of home grown food would immensely strengthen the position of the Empire. Besides there , are several millions of acres of land which want afforestiug, giving several hundred thousand of foresters work. All the rings of unused land l round every town would come into use, so that we can easily understand that the single taxer is right who said we would immensely profit if even all the proceeds of. the single tax were sunk into the sea, simply by breaking land monopoly and through it raise I wages to the true limit, causing jobs to hunt workers instead of now workers bunting jobs. Tax food and you hit the consumer of food, tax commodities and you I hit the consumer of commodities, tax land values and you hit the consumer of laud values, the landlord! _ .

British Women's Temperance Association. A number of the members of the above Society journeyed by 'bus to Hall Nook on Thursday after- noon, at the invitation of Mrs, Garnett. Being favoured with fine weather, the time was spent most pleasantly in wandering over the spacious garden. The great variety of roses were much admired as well as the herbaceous borders and hot houses. Tea was served in the dining room, and a short meeting held in the drawing-room, when the Secretary (Mrs. Simpson) read a report of the Annual Council meeting held in London: She also gave an interesting account of her visit to Castle Howard, York, one of the beautiful homes of the Countess of Carlisle, who invited all the members of the National Executive to stay with her from the 13th to 18th of July. There were 142 guests and a very happy week was spent in wander- jug over the beautiful park, in driving and boating. i The Castle was full of interesting works of art and a large collection, of pictures by the best masters there being some very fine paintings by Lord Carlisle. The party was photographed in front of the Castle. The Countess presented each delegate with photographs of herself, and she and her :daughter, who had been most admirable hostesses, ' seemed sorry when the parting time came. Mrs. , Garnett was thanked for her kind hospitality. Mrs. Owen, president, gave out a hymn. Rev. Sidney Pitt closed with prayer. A few roses were given to each , at the departure by 'has for home.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Cricket. Cresswell, the Warrington professional, took a well- earned benefit on Saturday and it was pleasing to see the home supporters show their high appreciation of his work for the club by assembling in such large numbers. Moreover Cresswell delighted the crowd by distinguishing himself with flee batting and bowling displays. The fhture was a League match with St. Helens and the Warringtonians had the satisfaction of registering a highly creditable victory. Going to the wicket first they amassed the substantial total of 185 and then had no difficulty in tumbling out the men from glassopolis for the insignificant figure of 58.

Cresswell has rarely been seen in better form. He batted brilliantly and had knocked up 73 before Tickle brought off an easy catch at the wicket. His chief hits were seSen 4's and four 3's. W. H. Podinore also helped materially to swell the Warrington aggre- gate, his flee innings realizing 43. He played in his most sparkling style and made five 4's.

The SL Helens men could make no headway against the bowling of Cresswell and Callon and the only players to reach double figures were J. Moss and W. Tickle with 13 and 18 not out respectively. Cresswell bowled with deadly effect and captured 7 wickets for 21 runs—a splendid performance. H. Callon was responsible for 3 wickets for 25 runs.

Warrington 2nd were unfortunate in having to—go to St. Helens with nine players. It is more than likely that had they been at full strength they would have triumphed. As it was, victory rested with the home eleven by the narrow margin of 18. On the winning side S. Burrows was in great form with the willow and placed 57 not out to his creiit. For Warrington A. Thewlis gave a capital display, his contribution being 43.

• The Warrington and District. League played a return match with the North Liverpool League on Monday and again secured the honours. In the first innings Howard secured five wickets for four runs and accom- plished the hat trick. Warrington soon passed the Liverpool score, J. Duckworth batting splendidly for his 21. Kneale for the visitors bowled a splendid length and had the creditable analysis of eight wickets for 10 runs. The visitors again offered a feeble resistance in their seco.nd essay, and were dismissed for 25. After the match the visitors were entertained at lunch at the Lion Hotel, and congratulatory speeches followed.

St. James's retain their proud position at the the head of the Warrington and District League, with Bewsey Wesleyana second. On Saturday the Saints had no difficulty in disposing of Rylands's,who gave a sorry display, not a single player attaining double figures. For St. James's Holt and Cummins battel well for 20 and 18 not out respectively, while J. Hallam took six wickets for nine rims.

Warrington Municipal Officers' Guild eleven are having a good season and on Saturday they triumphed over Latchford Blptists 2nd. There were, howover, only five runs to span. B. Green was the top scorer for the winners with 18, while A. Bramhall knocked up a creditable 35 for Latchford. Green also howled splendidly,taking seven wickets for 25.

Latchford Bsptists visited Rusholme and trounced the Congregationalists in no half hearted style. The home team were impotent against the deliveries of Cox and Warhurst, the first-named taking fix wickets for five runs, and Warhurst three wickets for three runs. T. Albinson and T. Dixon Vatted finely for the visitors.

Grappenhallnad a good week-end, for on Saturdly they defeated Altriucham Wesloyans and on Monday they proved more than a match for Ashton Elves. On Saturday, Gifford_ gave a capital bitting display for 27, while on Monday W. Carter made 15 in good style.

Congratulations to Pearson and Knowles on their victory in the Works Competition. They had doughty opponents in Walker's Brewery but succeeded is annex- ing first honours,their innings realizing 72 for 6 wickets against Walker's 51. Mr. Dodds again did daty for P. & K. but did dot g 9 to the wicket. Do was, however, alert in the field and brought off a very fine catch. W. Bennett (29), .T. Tarbuck (13 not out) and J. Thompson (11) were the highest scorers for the winners, while 11. Cook (10) topped the list for Walker's.

div.head: Bawling.
div.p: Bawling.

Warrington has become famous in the bowling world and it is certainly a matter for pride that two of our local teams have fought their way to the float for the club charnpilenship of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Bolfling Association. On Saturday, both the Warrington Cemetery and the Bull's head accounted for their opponents in the semi-finals, and next Satur- day they will try conclusious for the much coveted honours at Urmston. It will be a battle royal and which ever team proves victorious will deserve the success, for the players on each side will strain every nerve to win. Bull's' Head were also in the bust last year, when they were beaten on the Northumberland green by Pendleton (Belmont) ' after a tough struggle. With two teams hailing from the same district, in fact there are only about 440 yards between the greens, there is sure to be a grand fight for the cup and medals, and it is expected that a large crowd will he watching when they step On to the green at the Victoria Hotel, Urruston.

As to last Saturday's games, Bull's Head beat Waite- field by sheer good., play—a point which all who witnessed the game will readily concede. It was expected by most followers that thero would ba-a very close finistras 'both' tearns were cOnfidatit of figuring in the final. However, Whitefield were never in it after the brothers Weave came MI, winning—Albert by,2l-11 and Joe 21-7.1. The latter played the best game of the day for his side, whilst on the losing side H. Crossley undoubtedly took-the hononn by lea,iing, such a good .phiyer aSE.g...'aaw standing at 12. Crossley ran straight from 13-12 to game, and this by salendid play.

3. W. Ashton is an old coanty player, but he was-not up to his form on'Saturchy. Lie had a nio lead at 15-10 against J. Swanton, but could only score two' more, whilst his oppmeut ad led the 11 wanted.

W. Andrews did a remarkable feat against R. Eat- wood. The latter started well, and at the tenth end he led n-3. Then 'ea.cne a wonderful change. Andrews got in at the next end. and playing straight across the centre of the green actually ran right out, thus gaining -a really flee win by 12 chalks.

J. SenningS and Fogg each gained narrow wins for Warrington. The former had E. Taylor for an oppbnent, and this game lasted 33 ends and resulted, after a good et-to, in Taylor just lasing by 2 points' Fogg got 'home 212-18. HIS opponent was'W. Cranslaaw, who is still one of Valatetleld'o'best exponents of the game. The worst end he played was the last one, when the game was 19-18 against him, He lasi 11; yards to win in, and two yards to save-two, but he failed badly. - -

In the- match between Warrington Cemetery and Unsworth Conservatives there were some very one- sided games, three of the Unsworth tam and one of Cemetery team only getting single figures. Tom Ellison still maintains his form, and in beating 11. Morris 21-1 in 18 ends he showed some of tho best play of the afternoon. A. Scott is another who can generally bn depended upon. He and T. Maxwell played a close game up to 11-12, but then Scott went ahead, and at the finish was 7 p)ints to the good.

The seoond 'best wim was gained by A. Shepherd, of Ensworth, who defeated one of %Torrington's youngest players, R. Antrobus, 21-5, running from 10-5 to game. A. J. Jones and S. Berry was also a short bout, Jones playing in something like his old form and only allowing Berry to register 7, whilst going to 21. R. Rothwell led all the way against E. Warburton, never allowing him to draw level and finally gaining a 9 point win.

Two young Warringtonians in A. Forster and J. Gleavo just managed to win,the former by 1 and Weave by 4. Forster was behind at 17-20, but playing up for all be was worth won as stated above. G. Ball, jun., fairly ran away from E. Openshaw, who only scored 5 chalks. Ball showed something like his true form and was full value for his big win.

A pleasing feature of the match was the play of the genial proprietor of Cemetery Hotel, J. Allison, who playing against T. Bleakley; won very easily. At the tenth end the game was 8-7 in his favour, and from there he ran to 15-7, and finally finished 21-9.

Much interest centred in the last of the county games under the auspices of the British Crown Green Association to decide the holders of the Crosfleld Cup for twelve months and also the winners of the medals which took place at Wolverhampton between Yorkshire and Staffordshire on Bank Holiday. Thehon. secretary of tte association took the cup, so that Stafforshire might see what was being played for. The match resulted in a win fot Yorkshire by S:i points, which leaves Lancashire the champion county for 1908, they haring won all their matches and coming out with the best aggregate over Yorkshire: Mr. President Coombs and the Lancashire and Cheshire Association are to be congratulated on the result, and it goes without saying that the president of the L. and C., Mr. A. H. CrostWd, M.P., will also be delighted that his county should be the first holders of the Cup.

The Warrington Works Competition closes to-day when there will doubtless be a keen struggle for the trophy between Whitecross No. 1 and L.& N.-W. The wire men carried off the honours last year so that naturally they are very hopeful, but the L.& N.-W. are deter- mined to do their utmost to alter the destination of the I cup.
~ton.
On Saturday L. & N.-W. met Pearson and Knowles and, after an interesting match, defeated them by 11

p la ts. A capitt came was that bce we I J.Holland Gibson carried all before him fore long Um' ' but his opponent gradually gained on him and they were level at 13. Gibson, however, maintained his good forta and securing two singles ran Oct winner by 15-13. G. Ball, the forge men's captain, could not get going and was beaten by R. Marrow to the tune of 15-6. E. Taylor, the railway capta'n, did better, accounting for J. Hardman by 15-11.

Whitecross had not much difficulty in administering the quietus to Ryland; N. 1; the majority being just GO. There was a very interesting encounter between G. Holbroo:i(Rylands captain) and Ted Gleave.The players were on equal terms at 8,9, and 11, and then Holbrook I got in two and led 13-11. Gleave, however, had things all his own way to the end and won by 13-15. A. Gleave (Whitecross captain) had an easy task in accounting for It. Savoury by 15-5. A close game between G. Warburton and A. Stringer attracted much attention. Stringer led 11-7 and 12-9, but Warburton was on his mettle and placed himself ahead by 14-12. Stringer's next effort made the contestants equal and then Warburton gained the necessary 1 and triumphed by 15-14.

The President's main in connection with the Cemetery Hotel Club was decided on Nlenday, and resulted as follows :-1, T. Ellison; 2, Hill ; 3, J. Gibson ; 4th, %V. Cottam • sth, J. Howarth ; 6th, F. ; 7th, A. Bothwell ; Bth, W. Barton; 9th, it. Trin•'ger ; 10th, E. Littlewood ; 11th, A. Williams ; 12th, 'f. Harrison ; 13th, G. Ball, sen. ; Uth, W. Taylor ; 15th, J. Wood; 16th, H. Rathbone.
Rugby Football. Do not fail to get a copy of our Football Annual and Sports Record, which is on sale at ali newsagents to-day.

-- 1 Football Club practices commenced on Thursday ' evening, and from now till September 5, the men wilt 'be busy getting fit for the fray. No new IVarrington captures are announced yet. Wigan have signed on W. Johnston (one of the best of the All Blacks forwards) in addition to L. 13. Todd, and have also secured Gunn, the. Bradford full back. Where there's a parse there's a way.

div.head: SOiIPH LANCASHIRES IN CAMP. Strenuous Days on the Hills.
div.p: SOiIPH LANCASHIRES IN CAMP. Strenuous Days on the Hills.

On IllondlY the endurance of the troops of the South Lancashire Brigade, which includes the Warrington Territorials, under canvas at Knock-aloe, Peel, was put to a very severe test. The operations extended for seven or eight hours over ground which, to put it mildly, is not a little rugged, and during the whole time the heat of the sun was almost tropical in its intensity. To make matters worse, the men were entirely without rations, and had, indeed, nothing whatever to eat, not even a biscuit, from early breakfast until the return to camp ;Ines five o'clock.

_ _ _ As might have been expected, the test was ton severe for some of the less seasoned youngsters, and quite a number fell out on the line of march, while in addition there were several slight cases of heat apoplexy. Indeed a few of the casualties did not return to camp until two or three hours after the main bodies had arrived, and the organisation of search parties was at one time being seriously considered, ambulance waggons being actually sent out to pick up the stragglers. In the end, however, every man was accounted for, and it may be said that the great majority of the troops have derived considerable benefit from the test, and by the end of the training will be as hard as the proverbial nail.

Tuesday's operations, although in length almost quite the same, were much less arduous than those on Mon- day. For one thing, the temperature was considerably lower, the sky being somewhat thickly overza.st the whole day, while a few slight but very refreshing showers fell at intervals. Moreover, the men took a meat ration with them and cooked it on the field, so that when they got back to camp they were all as fresh as paint. ,• Incidentally it may be said that all ranks have got quite expert in this matter of ,cooking their own food. On the drst occasion they set. about the job in very amateurish fashion, and were, it must be confessed,very ' dubious about the result ; bet now they get to work as if the building of tiny area in the open and the con- version of their canteens into miniature cooking stoves were longstanding items in tlie daily routine. Although the men are working so hard, they are, at the same time, thoroughly enjoying. themselves. They have plenty of leisure for recreation -in the open, and mimes of all kinda are organised. The cheap trips to Douglas and other places are also well patronised ; while, as is ever the CASe, the large marquee of the Young Meri's Christian Association is a never-failing attraction.

Au incident in the operations on the mountains is worthy of special record._ A private of Captain Owen's company was giwen a written message with the order to take it quickly to Colonel I;'airclough,\ who was at a farm some mile and a half away. When he arrived panting at the farm the' golonel was not there, so that he had another mile to go to get his message delivered. . Hurrying on he found the Colenel,clelivered his message and promptly fainted. The mita was rather ill in tamp the same eight, but allltdreire his pinch-. - Wednesday was a day of comparative rest—comPara- tire, that is to a es', when the arduous nature of the operations of lalonday and Tuesday is taken into con- sideration ; for, although not engaged in brigade work on ths.hills,•tho troops were very far'frorn idle. Dining the day there were several distinguished visitors, notably Lord Raglan, Lieutenant-Governer of the island ; Sir Charles Barnett, .general certircander-in-chief of the western command ; and—the colonel or the Genera! Staff West Lancashire Division, Drill was chiefly under corps arrangement, but in the course of the cltty a selected company from each battelion competed for the hand- some challenge cep presented to the brigade two years ago by Mr. Francis Howard, and which, at Llanberis, in .Au,geatlast, was won by C Company of the present 9th : General Barnett's visit to Knoel:nlee was not made out of mere curiosity. He went the rounds of the whole camp, looked in at the variOns stores, 'kitchens, canteens, and sergeants' messes, and everywhere in his kindly way put Pertinent questions. 'Whether or no he was fully satisfied with everything he saw the • writer cannot say, but no doubt-ho was, seelug that although the arrangements of the camp may in some minor particulars fall a little short of perfection, there is nothing to be found amiss in the state of the lines, in the discipline that is everywhere maintained, or in the conduct of the rank and file whether on or of! tint.y. Another item on Wednesday's programme was the inspection by •an • officer ,detailed by the County of Lancaster Association of the clothing and equipment of all the troops under canvas. The •inspection was very thorough, and the older clothing was condemned whole- sale. It was indeed made _plainly evident that the association does not intend tO allow the troops of the county to remain in possession of any kind of gear which is at all Out of data Or in any way unsuited for active service.

The 'Vartity sing -song in the Y.q.C.A. marcpsee on Tuesday night was a huge success. The tent itself was filled to overflowing, while the curtains on one side having been taken down, the inen gathered in hundreds outside to enjoy the excellent and varied progfamine. Among the visitors were the brigadier and the brigadier. major, both of whom during the evening spoke of the splendid work which is being carried on by Mr. Ross, the ever-courteous superintendent, and his zealous staff of honorary assistants. An interesting ceremony has talon place in camp, Sergeant-Instruction Newall,of the Warring toallittal ion having been presented with his bag service medal by the Brigadier, who shook hands with the Sergeant and congratulated him on his excellent record of service. The South Lancashire Brigade bad son Thursday the 'finest experience of the fortnight's training. Accom- panied by Medicals from Barrow, fienclal,and Blackpool who were attached to each battalion, they had a big day on the mountains, sometimes among the clouds, when telegraph stations were temporarily cut off from com- munication with the outer world. Captain Crostleld, of Warrington, who during the late war went to the front, described the day's operations as most instructive, testing the intelligence of all ranks. Several accidentroccurred daring the mancenvres. An ambulance waggon toppled over,braising the riders, NiV hill) a herssruan was thrown, breaking his collar-bone. THE RETURN. The Warrington Territorials are expected to arrive home about noon to-morrow (Sunday).

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

The members-of this Guild ;pent a very pleasant time on Bank Holiday. In the morning over forty of them, including the Rev. Sidney and Mrs. Pitt, and two vice-presidents,3lessrs. W. Winstanley and J. Mitchell, assembled in the grounds, adjoining the Cairo-street Unitarian Church, to have -their photo- graph taken. When completed, the photograph will be presented to Mr. Pitt on his impending departure from this circuit for Leeds. In the early afternoon a party, numbering over thirty, entrained for Frodsham. From there a delightful route was taken over the Overton Hills and through the woods, clothed in a wealth of lovely foliage, to lielsbr. A astiff climb up the bill brought the party to Armers Lake Farm, where, with appetites sharpened by the long walk, the members of the Guild pat took of an excellent tea. Afterwards the party separated. One group, after plunging through a mass of bracken, and singing several well-known hymns, were disappointed in finding themselves at the point from which they had started. However, the summit of the bill was reached after walking through the fields. The view was enchanting and called forth exclamations of delight. IThen came the tumbling, scambling descent of the t heather-clad hill, and it was a merry, though some- what tired, party which arrived in Warrington shortly before nine o'clock.

div.head: FOR LOVE OR LITCRE?
div.p: FOR LOVE OR LITCRE?
rALT, nIGUTS RESERTED.I
BY GrY BOOTHBY,
Author of "Dr. Nikola," "Pharos, the Egyptian,* "A Bid for Fortune," "The Marriage ol Esther," "A Sailor's Bride," &c.

When Dick Ileinsworthy, the doctor of Great aad Little Septon, asked pretty Molly Carew, the lawyer's daughter, to marry him, he little knew the issues that would result from that apparently harmless question. Still-less did he guess that more than a hundred and fifty years later I should nnearth the story of his love affair, and should, worse still, make capital out of it. From what I have been able to gather from the perusal of certain diaries—the writing in which is almost illegible —and from a considerable amount of correspondence (in which it is necessary in many cases to read between the lines, either rightly or wrongly, according to one's judgment), Lawyer Carew must have been a man of violent temper, a stern husband, a hard father, and, not to put too fine a face upon it, as miserable an old hunks as ever went out of his way to save guinea. That he should, therefore, have come safely off the rocks he had himself constructed, seems scarcely to be in the fit and proper order of things.
TO. begin with, there can be no doubt that Hems-

worthy Proposed to, and was accepted by, Molly, as they walked home from church oft a certain June evening in the year 1743. His diary also records the fact that, later on the same evening, he "let blood for Squire Edgebathe, of the Hall," little dreaming, poor fellow, that. the gentleman in question was destined to die the week following, and by so doing would cause him, for a time at least, the greatest uneasiness he had ever known in all the eight-and-twenty years of his existenCe. Squire Edgebathe was, with the exception of a Maiden sister in London, the last of his race. At his death, therefore, the Hall was sold, and, as may be supposed, public opinion in the neigbour- heti:A was vastly concerned as to the antecedents and, shall we say, the possibilities, of the new owner. His name was Devereux, and it was generally understood that he had been for many years abroad in his Majesty's Colony of Virginia, where it was stated lie had amassed great wealth. Now, it must be understood that for a couple of yelre prior to the death of Squire Edgebathe the London-road, which runs through and connects Great and Little Septon, had been neld in subjec- tion by a notorious highwayman, known to fame as Hangman Jack. This unenviable sobriquet waft bestowed upon him by the neighbourhood when it became known that, on a certain memorable occasion at the commencement of his career, he had stopped and robbed the very individual whose duty it was to rid the world and society of gentlemen of h:s peculiar vocation. From what I have been able to discover, reading between the lines, rs I have already said, I am prepared to assert that the highwiryinan in question was not so popular in his district as he might have been. I gather that he kept himself too much to himself, except in the way of business, of course; did not frequent or patronise any of the local houses of call, and to all intents and purposes conducted himself as a modest, retiring gentleman, practising his profession without ostentation or any undue self-advertisement. None knew his real name, where he dwelt, or, indeed, 'anything con- cerning him—save that he had the misfortune to be hump-backed; that he was a consummate horse- man, and as fine a shot as ever put finger to trigger. Having now introduced you to pretty Molly Carew, whose portrait, hanging in the hall of her great-great-great-grandson's house proves her to have been a most charming young lady; to Lawyer Carew, her father; to Dr. Dick Hemsworthy ; to Squire Devereux, late of Virginia; and to Hangman Jack, the highwaymen, it would perhaps be as well that I should proceed with my story with as little delay as possible. To bark tack to the beginning of things let me again assert that Dick Hemsworthy, who, of course, should have been giving more attention to his profession than to love-making, was desirous of marrying Miss Carew. Accordingly, and I can imagine with what trepidation, he proposed, and being, as I have said, a handsome spark, was at once accepted. The young couple, however, happy though they were, had bargained withreff the lawyer, who, as the diary proves, was destined to make trouble for them, and at a very early date. He was a stern parent, was that nann of parchment; a man with an eager eye for the main chance and a particularly fine knack of getting his own way when 11 found himself in need of it. That he had much affection for his daughter I cannot convince myself. That he hoped and intended to marry her well, or, in other words, to profit himself through her marriage, I am as certain as a man can well be of anything. I have seen his portrait—hanging at the end of the room opposite that of his daughter —a thin, nut-cracker face, with a mouth that speaks for determination, and eyes that could be as hard as flint should their owner so desire. Indeed, as I stood before the picture I could find no difficulty in imagining the interview that took place in the lawyer's °Tice on the following mornirg. Hems- worthy pleaded with nil the eloquence at his command for the hand of the girl he loved so well; she, poor, motherless child, waited, tremblirg in the wainscotted hall for the verdict that was to mean everything, almost life itself, to her. The lawyer,- however, proved obdurate. Nothing the other could do or say would move him. With the brutality of a man who knows the worth of the treasure he possesses, he declined to part with her at such a price, while there might be more tempting offers waiting. It was in vain that the young man expostulated, promised, offered to settle all he possessed in the world upon the girl ; the obstinate I old father would not yield. What was worse, he vowed that lie would hear no more of the matter, and, finally losing his temper altogether, went even so far as to forbid Hemsvrorthy his house, tacking on to it the threat that, should he discover him upon the premises, he would order his servants to expel him forcibly. Such behaviour could have but one result. Heinsworthy was, without doubt, a high-spirited young fellow, and, what was more, one who was but little likely to endure patiently inch high-handed treatment. He invited the !awyer to inform him as to the grounds upon which . lie based his refusal. The old man, however, declined to answer either that question or any ether. It was sufficient, be declared, that he would not permit him to become his son-in-law. "Then listen to me," cried Hernsworthy, whose presence of mind had for the moment deserted him. "No, don't say that you won't hear me, for I tell you you shall. You have refused my suit, you have heaped insults upon me, but for Molly's sake I will forgive you. On one point, however, I am resolved. Come what may, she shall be my wife. She loves me and I love her. Nothing can alter that. Ido iot know what your ambition is so far as she is concerned, nor do I care. But this Ido know, she shall be no other man's wife but mine!" "Out of my house, sir!" shouted the other in a. paroxysm of fury. "If you value your life never dare to darken my doo,rs again. Marry my girl indeed! You puppy! She should not be your wife if you were the last man on earth. I'd rather see her in her grave first!" "Very well. Time will prove which of us is right," returned Hemsworthy, quietly picking up his hat and preparing to leave. "As I have already told you, I love her, and it will not be my fault if Ido not win her. At least I know that, happen what may, she will be true to me." "She'll do as I tell her, or I'll know the reason why," snarled the other. "As for you, you know what to expect if you dare to shew your face here again. Now he off with you!" "Think it over, sir, said Dick, turning to him again in one last appeal. "Try to realise that your only child's happiness depends upon your action. Don't drive its both to despair by a hasty answer, I implore you.. Remember that we love each other, as you must surely have loved at some period in your life. Your daughter is all the world I to me."

The irascible old gentleman, however, remained obdurate. No argument that could be brought forward would move him. He had set his mind against the marriage, and that was sufficient. Dick realised that it was on;y so much waste of time to continue the discussion. He accordingly left the room, and ptepared to return to his own abode in order to arran,e some scheme which should help him towards the attainment of his desire. This, however, as he very soon discorered, was destined to p!ova somewhat more dacult than be had

div.head: Examiner, Saturday August 8, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday August 8, 1908.

anticipated. • The old lawyer, backed by a couple of family servants, kept poor Molly a strict prisoner. She might air herself in the garden, which was enclosed by high walls, as much as she pleased, but beyond that circumscribed demesne she was on no account to go. She might weep her eyes out, beg for mercy as much as she pleased, her father was inexorable. He fortified himself and his opinions with much wine, and vowed that no sawbones should ever be son-in-law of his. As may be supposed it was not long before the crisis came, and this, so far as I can ascertain, is how it happened. , Squire Davereux, as the neighbourhood had by this time learnt to call him, chanced to have some legal business on hand which it was necessary should be arranged without undue delay. Believing that Lawyer Carew would serve his purpose as well as any other, he, one summer morning, called upon that gentleman. The interview was eminently satisfactory to both parties, and when it was concluded the lawyenproposed that they should crack a bottle together in honour of (Le event. They did so; and not one, but several. From what !I have been able to gather, ii would appear that the fourth cork had scarcely been drawn when pretty !Mistress Molly in her perambulation of the garden chanced to pass the window. As she herself describes it in a letter to a friend, written some months later, she was immediately "hailed into that odious presence!" The squire, thin, pale, cadaverous, with eyes like those of a snake, was seated in a high-backed chair beside the table. Ile paid her many compliniente, -.rowed that he had never been presented t:o so bewitching a beauty, and left the house, to all intents and-purposee, a man over head and ears in love. Next day lie called again. The day following found him cqualfy attentive. The lawyer was delighted. Here at last was a suitor after his own heart, rich, a hard hand at a bargain, n,iggardly, and a deep drinker. What mattered his daughter's opinions ? If the squire were in earnest, and was prepared with his settlement—egad! he should have her, or her father would know the reason why. Needless • to say the poor girl suffered agonies of terror. She hated the very sight of the squire, and I believe would rather have married poor Mad Peter. the village idiot, offhand than have been united to the owner of the Hall. That he—the latter—was. !determined to have her for his wife is a fact that !admits of no doubt whatsoever, as I will presently prove to you. He was a man of determination, and when he made up his mind on a subject he !usually managed to accomplish it, either by fair I 'means or foul. ! That she would decline to listen to his advances never crossed his mind. And yet she did, and with such vehemence that her father threatened her with the direst penalties of his wrath should she repeat her behaviour. He declared that she should marry the squire if he had to drag. her to church on her bended knees. Needless to say, the !poor girl's life at that time was very far removed Ifrom a happy one. • As for Heiusworthy lie was nearly beside himself. lie • believed and trusted his sweetheart implicitly, but he knew the power her father had over her, and be realised that, if , the old man made up his mind to force the marriage upon her, it would be well-nigh impossible for her to resist. What was worse he could flat see her or communicate with her: At last, when certain news reached his ears, he was unable to bear it any longer, so determine 4 upon a desperate stroke. Without any hope that good would result from I it, he made his way to the lawyer's house and I demanded an interview. Had it ben possible the !old fellow would have refused to see him, but !Hemsworthy was in his presence almost before lie was aware of the fact. --------

"What does this mean ?" he inquired, angrily, looking up from the deed he was perusing. "I thought I forbade 7ou to come to my house again?" "I have come to ask if this vile story is true," returned the other, speaking as calmly as wa3 possible under the circumstances. "What is the story?" asked the lawyer. "I pay no heed to gossip. "It is said that you have given your consent to a marriage between your daughter and Squire Devereux," said Dick. "Is that true?" . . .

"Quite true. What then ? What right have you to ask the question? Go away and mind your own business, young man, or you'll.find 'twill be the worse for you." "This is my business," retorted the other. "It concerns the happiness, not only of my life but of your child's also. She does not love this man ; she could not be happy with him. To link her life to his would be a cruel and inhuman action." "Matters would, of course, be reversed if I permitted her to marry you," sneered the lawyer. Then losing control of himself altogether he shook his fist in the young man's face, bade him be off about his business, and vowed that he would marry his daughter to whomsoever he pletsed, and that it would be the worse for anyone who should dare to come between them.

"Very good, sir," replied the young man, when the other had ceased his harangue. "I told you some weeks ago that I would marry your daughter, and I repeat it now. Rest assured of this, happen what may, Devereux shall not have her." With that he left the house and strode along the street towards his own abode in a towering rage with the squire, the lawyer, and everyone who shewed the least inclination to come between him- self and the girl he loved, -and whom he feared he was about to lose.

•- As ill-luck would have it, he was scarcely a hundred yards from his own front door, when he became aware of a man, who, mounted on a line black horse, was riding slowly towards him. One glance was sufficient to tell him that this individual was no less a person than Squire Devereux, his rival, and, at that moment, the greatest enemy he had in the world. As they came nearer they looked into each other's faces and what they saw there must have told its own tale. Squire Devereux had been drinking heavily that afternoon, and his :temper was soured in consequence. One glance was enough to inform the other that he was quite pre- pared to pick a quarrel with anyone, and with him- self in particular. Seeing his enemy before him he bade him get out of his way, raising his whip as if t 3 emphasise the order. Hemsworthy, however, did not alter his course. The words the old lawyer had addressed to him a few minutes before were still rankling in his mind. At the moment he desired nothing better than a chance of picking a quarrel with his foe. Seeing that he did not budge, Devereux struck hint a heavy blow across the shoulders with his whip. Then, with a cry of fury, Hemsworthy sprang upon him; dragged him from his saddle, and • seizing the whip, with which he had himself just been struck, thrashed him with it until fatigue , made him desist. Then, dropping the whip, he hurled a parting defiance at the prostrate man and strode on to his own abode. He quite realised the Important bearing his treatment of the squire wonld - have on his relationship with the Carew family, but his case appeared so hopeless that it ,did not seem as if anything could damage it further. I As it transpired, however, it served one good , purpose, for the squire' so soundly had he been trounced, was compelled to take to his bed, which he did not leave for upwards of ten days, Alms affording his rival time to make up his mind as to what course he should pursue for the betterment of his unhappy love-affair. That Devereux, as soon as he should be able to more *bout, would endeavour to get even with him, he had not the least doubt, but what tactics he would adopt he was quite unable to imagine. He was soon to find out, I however, and it is upon that discovery that the whole interest of my story turns. One fine September morning, just as the doctor , was preparing to mount his horse, preparatory to I riding out to a farm some few miles distant from the village, he was accosted by a tall, military- looking stranger, who requested the honour of an interview, Hemsworthy led him into the house, and once there inquired his business. It thereupon 'transpired that the other, whose name was O'Rourke, was an Irish Captain, a friend of Squire Devereux, and the bearer of a challenge from that enraged gentleman. "Ye've put a grievous- affront upon me honourable friend," remarked the Captain, puffing out his chest with importance; "and it will be , himself that will be happy to oblige ye, with sword' or pistol, when and where ye may please. 'Twill be a pretty affair; that's to say, if ye've any know- ledge of the weapons." Now, from what I have been able to gather from the perusal of the diaries and letters to which have already referred, I have come to the con- clusion that Hemsworthy was as plucky a young man as you would have been likely to find in all that countryside; at the same time, I do not fancy that the idea of this duel appealed to him in any way. The squire was known to be a fine pistol shot, and, as Dick argued, it was very probable that he would be equally proficient with the sword. How- ever, there was no way out of it. He 'had been ehalleneed to mortal combat, and, unless he desired to be branded as a coward, pght. It must, That Devereux would kill him if he oould manage it was unfortunately a matter that admitted of little or ao doubt. It would be en easy, and, moreom, a permanent way of riddirg

himself of a troublesome rival. The result, how. ever, was not destined to be as satisfactory as Imo would probably have wished. The duel took place in the small, tree-shaded Close behind the church; pistols were the weapons chosen, and within five minutes of his arrival on the ground, Hemsworthy was lying on his back in the damp grass with a bullet through his chest. How it was he was not killed outright will ever remain a mystery, but, though he was carried home in what was supposed to be a dying condition, and was orerated upon by a rival practitioner from the neighbouring town, he eventually managed to pull through. It was a touch-and-go business, however, and there were timeg alien pretty little Molly Carew deemed it extremely probable that she would never see her lover again. Fate, however, was going to prove kind after all, and, though the fact at the moment seemed incredible, he was destined to live to dance his children's children upott his knee and to know as much happiness as falls to the lot of most men.

On the day that be was permitted to leave his bed for the first time, a visitor was ushered into his presence. . To his amazement this visitor proved to be no less a person than lawyer Carew himself. Remembering what had taken place at their last meeting Dick received his guest with pliteness, but with no appreciable warmth. ' "You're not pleased to see me, Richard Hen:worthy," began the ed man, when he had anted himself in the chair which had been placed for him. "And I don't wonder at it. I did you an injustice, and I've come to say I'm sorry for it. I was a blind old bat, and I deserve all I have received." Dick stared at hue .1 astonishment. He had not heard any news of late, and in consequence /rid no notion of what the,other was referring to. However, one thing was seH.eviclent, and that w‘t% the .fact that the old man was extremely aizious to be friendly. "I fear I do not quite understand," said Dick, a tone of apology. "Yon must remember I have heard no news since I took to my bed." "Egad then you're not acquainted with the reat discovery that all the countryside has 'pen, buzzing about these three weeks past. Well, well! And to think 'that, after all that lris happened between us, I should be the one t.) tell you. You're acquainted with Hangman Jack "
_ _ "The highwayman t tire heard of him—who his not? Whom hie he robbed now ? "

"That, my lad, is just the tale I am about to .t.lll you. The evening after the day on which you were shot by Squire Limpet'', the squire ctme riding into the village, vowing that he had b•en stopped and robbed by Jack on Three Mile ILtath. Nothing would suit him but he must htve vengeance, and at once. The rascal had robbed him of his watch, fifty pounds in gold, aid, what was more, a parcel of valuable deeds that, unlike the other articles, could not be replaced." "The scoundrel! .13ut still I fail to see what one robbery has to do with me ?" "Patience, and you shall hear. Best assured eta it concerns you more vitally than you suppose —unless you no longer love my daughter ?" _
"Ah, you know well enough what my feelings are towards her. But proceed with your story, I beg. Since it concerns me I am all impatience to hear the end." _ _ _

_ "Well, you must. know that on the day following the robbery I have just described the squire appeared before, me at my office and informed me that he was that morning in receipt of a communicationi from his assailant of the previous night to the effect that as the deeds were of no use to him they would be returned on payment of the sum of three hundred guineas to any individual he might nominate, pro- vided always dust he—the squire—did not appear in person to claim them, and also that he passed his word of honour that his messenger should come alone. The place of meeeting was to be the Seven Yew Copse on the London-road, and the hour daybreak. As you may suppose, I immediately inquired What part he desired me to play in this adventure, whereupon he informed me that he was anxious to solicit my help. The whole question eventually resolved itself into this. Being short of cash, I was to find the necessary money to redeem the deeds, and also to attend at the appointed spot at the hour named to complete the transaction, taking in return a mortgage upon his estates until repayment of the amount should be made, with interest." - "I rein surprised that you trusted the fellow,' said Dick.

The old gentleman's eyes twinkled. "It would have been an excellent investment," lie replied, "had things turned out as I anticipated. Let me, however, proceed with my tale. Having agreed to the squire's proposal, and the necessary money being forthcoming, I, with some misgiv- ings, I must confess, mounted my nag and repaired to the appointed spot.. "I'was a cold, cheerleps dawn, a thick mist covering the Downs. As I drew near to the copse where, as arranged, I was to meet the rascal, I can tell you, my lad, I found ray myself wishing myself well away. At last the trees came into view, and a moment later a hump-backed man, wearing a visard, which concealed more than half his face, made his appearance from the shelter and approached Tee. In a gruff voice he asked the reason of my presence at such place and at such an hour. Whether it was the cold, or whether, as is more probable, it was a very genuine fear for my safety that caused it, I cannot say; 'tis certain, however, that my teeth, chattered in my head as I told hitn my business. "‘ Here are the papers to which you refer,' says he, holding up a roll of papers as he spoke. ' Now where's the money ? ' "I put my hand into my pocket where was one of the bags, and was about to give it to him. At that moment, however, the sound of • horse galloping • on the crisp turf of the downs reached my ears. "` You've betrayed me,' cried the man before me with an oath, and as he spoke he snatched a pistol from his pocket and fired full and fair at me. As you can see for yourself here is the hole in my hat made by the bullet. How it was he did not kill me, I shall never understand. Then turning, he ran back to the wood to the spot where his. horse was waiting. A moment lates he was mounted and riding out from among the trees. By this time the sound of horse's hoofs that I had heard before seas drawing closer. A minute later a tall man, and well-mounted, dashed by me, pistol in hand. Ile encountered Jack at, the edge of the wood. "• You're my prisoner,' he cried. Yield your- self, or you are a dead man.' "For an answer the other drew a pistol from his holster, pointed it, and pulled the trigger. The bullet went wide, but not so that fired by .the new-comer. When the smoke had cleared -away Jack was lying on his back, dead, upon the turf, and his horse was galloping off across the downs:

"'lt's a pity I didn't take him alive,' said the stranger. ' But it's better to have him this way than not at all. I've been trying to catch him these three years, but he has always managed to give me the slip. Now let us take a look under that mask. I've long wanted a glimpse of my fine gentleman's face. • "As he spoke he knelt beside the dead man and lifted the vizard that concealed his features. What do you think we found there?" Hemsworthy was unable to say. • "The face of Squire Dercreux of (he Hall!" replied the lawyer. "lie--and no other—uas Hangman Jack.
"But what about the deeds? rsked Dick, when he had recovered from his astotishment.

"There were no deeds," replied the lawyer. "The whole thing was a carefully-laid plot to rob me. The rascal had come to the end of his tether, and intended flying the country with my money. He knew the thief-taker was after him, and this was the plan he had hit upon to obtain the sinews of war necessary for his flight." "And Molly ? " "She shall speak for herself. 1 nave been taught a lesson. I wanted a rich eon-in-law, and came near being cheated by a rogue. I refused an honest man, and have come nearer still to being punished for my folly. As soon as you're about again, egad! we'll have a wedding, and ever afterwards we'll thank Heaven for our deliverance from that scoundrel, Hangthan Jack." "Amen to that," said 'Dick. "Amen, with all my heart." Then the old man left him and went out to find his daughter. "Just fancy, he might have shot papa," Molly remarked, some few weeks later, a propos of the incident on the Downs. "That would have been sad indeed, Per lover replied. "At the same time, though I have small rause to love him, I cannot help remembering that 1 am inaebtect, in a large measure, to that shot for ray wife, and for the happiness I know to-day. Which would seem to prove that from base things, good may occasionally result, - [Tux Exp.]

WARRINGTON Fire in Battersby-lane. At 3.5 on Saturday afternoon, information was • received at the Fire Station that a fire had broken , cut in some wooden sheds in Battersby-lane belonging Ito Mr. Hazeldine, plumber, Rm. The brigade were just leaving the station on their way to the fire when a messenger dashed up with the news that their services were not required as the flames had been extinguished. • Shop Theft at Warrington. John 11PGay, a stranger, was sent to gaol for fourteen days at, the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday for stealing two caps from the shop of Charles Mounfield, Winwick-street, on Tuesday morning. He was seen by an assis'!ant in the shop to take the caps from off a hook in the doorway. BABY CARRIIOE9 of every description.—J. ' S. GARLAND, 51 to 55,Bridge st.,Warringtoner:-Advt. Children's Sommer. Camp. The first batch of boys under the charge of Mr. and Mrs. Cox and officers arrived at Prestatyn on Saturday at 11 30 a.m. They number 100. The -week in camp has been thorongtly enjoyed for in addition to the usual rambles through a charming district,sports have been engaged in with zest. The children returned to Warrington last evening, leaving Prestatyn at 7.3 p.m. The cooking arrangements have been excellently carried out by Mr. and Mrs. Whitney and Miss E. Bost ock. Bank Park and Gardens. On Sunday the old conservatory in the gardens, near the Mill Hall, was opened to enable the public to inspect the annual show of gloxinias, which is the finest ever seen there. There are numerous varieties, and it is no exaggeration to say that the flowers are about as perfect as it is possible for them to be. Some of the blooms are exceptionally well developed, and have been deemed worthy of being photographed. The show of flowers in the beds alongside the Infirmary and near the Aquaria are also worth inspec- tion, and probably the gardens never presented a more beautiful picture. Great credit is due to the head gardener (Mr. Whitfield) and his assistants. PUBLIC BENEFIT UIsinERIPFFIII CLOCK POR BffisT BOOTS IN LANCASIIIRE.—Adyt.

Retirement of Superintendent Monaghan. Warrington will shortly lose the services of a popular and efficient police officer in the person of Superintendent Monaghan, who has been a member of the Borough Police Force since February, 1880, and has sent in his resignation to the Watch Committea. He has risen from the rank of constable, and has been successively sergeant, inspector and superintendent, having officiated in the last named capacity for ten years. He has performed his duties most diligently and has made many smart captures. During his long connection with the police force he has earned the respect not rnly of the Watch Committee, but of the Chief Constatles under whom be has served, the men, and townspeople generally,and he has the best wishes of all in his retirement.

Licensed Uictuallers' Association. The li.9th annual meeting of the Warrington 'and District Licensed Victuallers' Association was held the other day at the General Wolf Hotel, Church- street, the President (Alderman John Evans, in the chair. There was a full attendance of mebbers.— Alderman Evans, who has held the office for 17 years, was re-elected president.— Mr. Joseph Shillcock was re elected vice president ; Mr. R. Shacklady, hon. treasurer; Messis,J. Allison and R. Perdue, trustees;

Messrs. Arthur Denhem," George Finch, john Lee: Thomas Partridge, NV. Rogers, and ,Robert Walker, committee.—The auditors, appointed for the ensuing year were Messrs. Earle and J. E. Shaw.—Mr. Enoch Locker was re-elected secretary, and in thanking him for his services for the Past year the meeting voted him an honorium for special services rendered. TRAVELLING TRUNKS. DRESS BASKETS, ETC., large selection. reasonable prices.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger,sl to 55, Bridge st.,Warrington.—Atlvt. Bank Holiday. The August Bank Holiday of 1007 will long be remembered for the ideal weather conditions which favoured it from early morning until evening, there was brilliant sunshine and trippers enjoyed them- selves to their hearts' content at various popular resorts. There were heavy bookings to Liverpool, New Brighton, Southport Blackpool, Chester, Frodsham' North Wales, and the Royal Lancashire show at Manchester. Cyclists, motor cycles, and motor cars were much in evidence on the Cheshire roads, and the tram cars carried hundreds of passengers to the outskirts of the town. The Football Club Sports at Wilderspool proved a great attraction and the places of amusement in Warrington were crowded in the evening. Athletes Successes. At the Blackley Sports, on Saturday, A. Siddall, of Warrington A.C. (39), took second prize in the 400yds. handican, and in the mile flat handicap G. Watmough, A.C. (981, also of Warrington, took the first prize At the Irlam C.W.S. Sports, the following Warrington athletes were successful in winning prizes, viz. : 100yds. boys, Regan, 23; 2; 1005ds.' open, J. Griffiths, 11, 1; Joe Griffiths, 13f, 3; mile bicycle handicap, NV. Haut, 100, 2; half-mile bicycle, Hunt, 45, 3; obstacle race, ltarrison, 8, 1 ; Foster, lis, 2; 2201d5., J. Griffiths.—At the Prescot Sports on Monday, J. Whalley, A.C. (40), won the first prize in the one lap obstacle race. Atl Rainford Sports on Tuesday G. Watmough scored a further success in the half mile, being followed by T. Lightfoot. whom he conceded 21 yards and beat by two. A. Siddall was second in the 220 yards race.

Drowned Whilst "Jack-Sharping." Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Warrington Police Station on Wednesday, on the body of Walter Bcardman, the eight-year-Old son of Henry Boardman, of 18, John-street, who was drownel in a clay-pit at Latchford on Friday afternoon. The deceased,in company with a playmate named Carlisle, was fishing for "jack sharps" with a small net, when Boardman, in removing weeds, overbalanced and fell into th'e,,water, and before assistance arrivtid he sank. The body was afterwards recovered by a tram- conductor named Timperley.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and commended the actions of Tim perley and also of a witness named Massey who attempte4 to recover the body. The jury expressed the opinion that the pit ought to be securely fenced round. The Coroner remarked that there was no obligation on the owner of the pit, as it was more than fifty yards from thelighway. Still unsurpassed, PREMIER CYCLES at 6 guineas. —Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. P.S.A. Meetings. At the weekly meeting of the Wycliffe Society on Sunday, Mr, W. Beswick presided, and spoke upon "The obedience and disobedience of Saul." Saul was be said, greatly blessed in his obedience, but greatly discomforted in his disobedience, and that was a lesson to all of them to be obedient to God's will. Mr. W. W. Drewitt, of Stockton Heath, gave an address upon" The wise counsel of David." The Psalmist was a great student, both of Nature and the Spirit of God. He gave good counsel in his youth, and wise teaching in his older years. The duty of the older Christians of to-day was to live and teach the great Gospel of the Lord, and to inspire the younger disciples, to greater usefulness for the Lord. Mr. C. Healey and Mr. R.Mills also took part in the meeting and Mr. IV. Pearce presided at the organ. An open meeting of the Buckley-street Society was held on Sunday, and was presided over by Mr. E. A Sanders. The address was given by Mr. E. Wynne-Jones and Mrs. Simpson read the lesson. Miss J. Armstrong (contralto) gave a good tendering of "Nearer, my God, to Thee." Miss M. Plinston accompanied on the piano.

Bewsey-road Wesley Guild. The members of this Guild spent a very pleasant time on Bank Holiday. In the morning over forty of them, including the Rev. Sidney and Mrs. Pitt, and , two vice-presidents, Messrs. W. Winstanley and J. Mitchell, assembled in the grounds, adjoining the ; Cairo-street Unitarian Church, to have their photo- graph taken. When completed, the photograph will he presented-to Mr. Pitt on his impending departure from this circuit for Leeds. In the early afternoon a patty, numbering over thirty, entrained for Trodsbam. From there a delightful route was taken over the Overton Hills and through the woods, clothed in a wealth of lovely foliage, to Helsby. A stiff climb up the hill brought the party to Armers Lake Farm, I where, with appetites sharpened by the long walk, I the members of the Guild partook of an excellent tea. Afterwards the party separated. One group, after plunging through a mass of bracken, and singing several well-known hymns, were disappointed in finding themselves at dui point from which they had started. However, the summit of the hill was reached after walking through the fields. The view was enchanting and called forth exclamations of delight. Then came the tumbling, scambling descent of the heather-clad hill, and it was a merry, though some- what tired, party which arrived in Warrington shortly before nine o'clock.
