MY DEAR

have been most.pleh.sed with the essays 3n "The Ideal Holiday" sent by members. Especially the ones dealing with places that I know well from personal experience have given great pleasure. I hope to receive some more, as the time as I write this has hardly expired. I want the full addresses of Maud Mobley and Amelia Brisley, winners in the Conundrum Competition; will these members kindly send their addresses, and I will imme- diately forward their prizes? Now I want you to tell me what you consider the best subject for a competition—not too diffi- cult, and open to girls and boys. The first prize is a nice silver watch. This is well worth taking a *little trouble to win, and I am sure the successful one will be highly pleased with the prize. Think out a competition,- and write and tell me all about it. With love, UNCLE NED.
—+— My ideal holiday place is Colwyn Bay. X have been there, and I had an enjoyable holi- day. I saw the beautiful scenery and also many curious ,things. MATJDE ENTWISLE•

People's ideas may differ as to an ideal lion. day. Some would like a fashionable seaside resort, while others would prefer the solitude of country lanes and the shade of the woodlafids. but my, ideal holiday would be in a different place from either of these. I think nowhere so thoroughly enjoyable for a month's holiday as "The Lake District," which would be my kleaL It is pleasant to get into the train, expectant of the joys to come, and to be carried swiftly away from the bustle of the town to the sweet, fresh country. Arriving at Windermere, what _

joy we feel as we walk through the streets of the little town, and notice the quiet tOwnsfolla busy at their daily work, and to remember that we have a whole month's holiday before us! We are weary with our journey, so we do not go far to-day, but quickly•find our way ,to the little hotel at Bowness, which overlooks the lake.

The next day we go on a tour round the place. How delightful the air feels, and how lovely Lake Windermere looks, as we view it from the landing-stage, lying calin and peaceful, sur- rounded by the grand old mountains! Retracing our steps through the town, and passing the Station, we ascend Orrest Head, from which may be seen a view of the whole thirteen miles' length of Lake Windermere. One is able to distinguish the different moun- tains by looking at a pictorial chart in 6 glass case on the summit of this hill. Langdal Pikes stand out most prominent, while here and there on the thickly-wooded mountains surrounding the lake may 'be seen various residences of gentlemen, many of the houses being built of white stone, which makes a great contrast to the dark green fir trees. From this height the little lake steamers look like flies crawling across the surface of the water.

Some time later on our -,holiday we are being borne along in a steamer, ; whilst the sweet chords of a harp are wafted across the lake to us by the soft, fresh breezes. We arrive at Ambleside, at the northern end of the lake. This is a very victuresque little village, the only thing out of place amid its mountain scenery being its modern church, which was designed by Sir Gilbert Scott, and is not in harmony with its rugged surroundings. Later on in our visit we go to Rydal and Grasmere, passing on our way the "Poet's Seat" over- looking Rydal Water, where the "Lake Poet; Wordsworth, composed many of his beautiful nature poems. Then on. to Grasmere, where we I may visit Wordsworth's old home, "Dove I Cottage," with its many memorials of his resi- dence in the district, also the quaint little church and graveyard where he is buried. On other days we visited LA,ely Keswick and Der- wentwater, with its Ruskin Memorial on Friars' Crag. Day after day we found opportunities of visiting Ulleswater and Thurlmere, which gives its water to Manchester City. Buttermere, Crummack, and Honiston Pass, all revealing fresh wonders, too many to mention in "detail. We can hardly realise that a month can have passed so swiftly, and now it is the last day. The train steams out of the station, and as it turns a bend we see Windermere in all its splendour lay shimmering, bathed in the rays of the setting sin. Thus the curtain falls on our happy time, leaving but the golden threads of memory to be linked into one, great chain of remembrance, as we recall all the joys of our "Ideal Holiday." DOROTHY STARKE.

div.head: VISIT OF THE AUSTRALIAN TEAM.
div.p: VISIT OF THE AUSTRALIAN TEAM.
Interesting Particulars.

Some interesting facts as to the Australian team of professional footballers who will be touring the Northern Union constituency next season has been ft.rnished through the reading of a letter from Australia. The writer was Mr. J. J. Giltinan, the hon. secretary of the New South Wales Rugby League, who, it is under- stood, will have charge of the team in its tour. His letter, which is dated Sydney, June 15th, reads :—" I arm in receipt c.f your letter dated 22nd April, and I am pleased that your Committee is in favour of our sugges- tion with reference to the test matches, and we feel confident that our Australian boys' will give a good account of themselves. We arrive in England on Sep- tember 27th, and the first match is to be arranged for October 2rd, finishing the tour on March 7th. We leave Australia by the P. and O. liner Macedonia on August 15th. We intend bringing 30 members, and they will be the best the Australian Rugby League can produce. No doubt you have heard the results of matches played against the All Blacks," the New South Wales boys having beaten them on three occasions." Referring to the third match, Australia v. New Zealand. the writer says it was indeed, a pretty game, and all the local papers predicted a successful time for the Australian team while on tour in 'England. He continues :—We are also playing the All Maori ' team, which is a fine body of men. We played them on June Bth in the presence of 30,000 people. Again the boys in blue ' asserted their superiority by beating the Maoris by 18 points to nine. The exhibition of foot- ball was of the highest, and I may inform yen that the Northern Union game is taking on' in New South Wales and Queensland. I wrote von before, and told you that it would not be our fault if we were uot the leading attraction in Australia, and these predictions to-day are fulfilled." • As an instance of this the writer compares the support accorded the Northern Union game and that of the Rugby Union (Amateur) body. He says : "The Rugby .Union test matches were played on the best ground in the world—that is, the New South Wales Cricket Ground. The Rugby Union brought country players from all round, the number being ten districts, which sent twenty men each. From these teams they selected what they called their test' team, and from this team the test' team is to be selected to tour England. They advertised it and boomed it for all it was worth, and their prices were 6d. admission and Is. grand stand—a thing they never did before in the history of Australia—and they had the 'magnificent' attendance of 1,000 people at the outside. On our ground, as I before stated, we had 30,000 people who paid ls. to the ground and 2s. to the grandstand, so you may judge for yoursalves the Northern Union game is well established in New South Wales. No doubt you heard of the sad death of the secretary of the 'All Black' team, Hr. A. 11. Baskerville, who died on tour at Bris- bane. We had to thank him for the inception of the Northern Union game in Austral ia,for had it. not been for the 'All Black' team visiting your country. I don't suppose the Northern Union game would have been heard of in Australia to-day. The All Black' team are playing a match for the benefit of the mother of Mr. BRekerville on June 13th, at Wellington, and I am pleased to say the Rugby Union (Amateurs) have post- poned all their matches, giving this particular matoh the full benefit of their attendance. If you have not already been informed of it, the Rugby League of Australia have elected your humble servant. J. J. Giltinan, as manager of their team to go to England, and in doing so have conferred upon him the highest honour possible." The professional team will be captained by H. H. Messenier, well-known as one of the " stars " of the last Colonial team to visit England. The tour will commence at Mid-Rhonddlion October 3rd, and of the representative matches to be arranged one will be played in London and another on the Ooodison Park ground at Everton., For the first few weeks of their tour the Australians will make Manchester their head- quarters.

NATIONALIZATION Ole RAILWAYS.

At the last monthly meeting of the Council, the President (Mr. Holman Kingdom, M.A.) in the chair, communication was read from the Railway Nationaliza- tion Society, inviting the co-operation of the Chamber In promoting the policy of the acquisition and management of the railways of the United Kingdom by the State, and pointing out the numerous anomalies and inconveniences attaching to the present systems An interesting discussion took place, in which some difference of opinion was manifested, and it was finally resolved that the Secretary write to the Society intimating that the Chamber was not, at present, prepared to adopt their proposal. DAYLIGHT SAVING BILL.

The President having explained the proposals embodied in the above measure, and emphasised the advantages, It was moved by Councillor J. FULTON. SMITH, seconded by Mr. Jams BRANDRETH, and unanimously resolved :—" That the Council of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce approves, in prin- ciple. of the provisions of the Daylight Saving Bill now before Parliament, believing that the carrying of these into effect cannot but be of benefit to the com- munity at large, and particularly to those connected with industry and commerce. They further hope that the Bill may take its placn on the Statute Book at an early date, and request the Secretary to send a copy of this resolution to the President of the Board of Trade and to the local Members of Parliament."

div.head: SIR REDVERS BULLER'S ESTATE.
div.p: SIR REDVERS BULLER'S ESTATE.

The will ot General Sir Redvers Buller has been proved in the Exeter Registry Court. The gross value of the estate is sworn at £34,992, the net value of personal estate being £32,488. The piece of plate pre- sented to Sir Redvers by the county of Devon, the lamps presented to him by.the Frontier Light Horse, and the clock and vases presented to him by Baker's Horse, and two shields presented to him by the ladies of Cape Colony are to pats as heirlooms. th Redvers expresses the hope that his successor at Downes will continue to those in receipt of them, and grant to any hereafter worthy of them, the allowances he had made to the old servants and workmen on the estate.

I think an ideal holiday would be to go to C'kina for a fortnight of my month, and see all the queer distoms of the people They have such different ways from ours that 'it would be both amusing and in- teresting to see them. My next week I should like to spend in London among the slums. I should enjoy very much to see the poor little children (who never see or hear anything but dreadful things) enjoy the pleasures of a day's outing in the country. The last week of my holiday I should like to spend in Westward Hol to enjoy th• many pleasures of the seaside. BESSIE LEWIS.
110 W I SHOULD LIKE TO SPEED MY SUMMER HOLIDAYS:
BEAUTIFUL JERSEY.

_ I should like to spend a month's holiday at Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands. The two principal routes to the Channel Islands are via Southampton and Weymouth. There is a steamer which stills during the night, and one which sails during the day. I should prefer to go in the day-time, leaving Weymouth at 1.45 in the afternoon, and reaching Jersey at 7.45 in the evening. • Jersey is noted fog its beautiful scenery, and a great deal of my time would be spent in walking and going for picnics. Nearly every day sea-bathing and fishing would occupy my attention. I should also go for several cycling tours,and would also take advantage of the excursions which run between Jersey and Guernsey. Excursions are also run between Jersey and France, and if the opportunity occurred a week-end visit might even be paid to "La Belle France."

St. Helier is the capital of Jersey, and naturally a few days would be spent there loOk- ing at the shops and different buildings and visiting its churches. St. Aubin, once the, port of Jersey, would also, be visited. There are several very fine parks in Jersey, and it would be a great pity to miss visiting them. I should also make a point of seeing Mont Orgueil Castle, noted for its historical connections. MARGARET MARY PRESS.

A month of my holiday this year I -should like to spend exactly as I please. The follow- ing are the places I should visit. The town of St. Alban's, in Hertfordshire, would be my first week's stoppage, for that town is very famous in English history; It.is the spot where three thousand Yorkists defeated the troops of King Henry the Sixth, in the year 1455. For' the other three weeks I should return to London, where I should find much to interest me, for London is a very ancient city. I should visit the town of Waterloo, where Wellington so bravely fought with and defeated Napoleon Bonaparte. Then it was that Napoleon was forced to give up his throne, and so France was yielded up to England. I think every one who has any interest in history would want to see such places as these. Then I should want to take a peep at Kensington Palace and West- minster Abbey, the latter being the grand old Abbey where our late Queen Victoria was crowned. There were great rejoicings all over the country on that occasion, for the French General, Marshal Soult, no longer a foe, was present to drink the health of England's Queen. Then at the "White City," now that it i's opened, I should put in an appearance, where it would take quite a week to see all the sights which that possesses. The wonderful machinery, for instance, and the Indians, and the style in which they have their meals. Then my last visit would be to St. Paul's Cathedral, where the remains of so many of our English heroes rest. The monument I should mostly wish to see is Nelson's, for a greater hero England never had, anal, the only reward a grateful country 'could give him was a lasting monument in the lofely old Cathedral men- tioned above. I think after I had thoroughly inspected these delightful places my month would be well on the wane, and my destination then would have to be, home and school. - ALBERT ARNOLD.

div.head: IDEAL HOLIDAY-LONDON.
div.p: IDEAL HOLIDAY-LONDON.

I am writing to tell you how I should like to spend my holidays. Having never been to London, I should like to visit the town. London is the vast metropolis of the British Empire. During the last decade of the event- ful nineteenth century it attained proportions which eclipse those of any other city, either in the ancient or the modern world. When 1 should arrive at Waterloo Station, I should stroll across Waterloo Bridge, and view the " silent highway" of the Thames; then trace the tree-lined terrace of the Victoria Embank- ment, and within ten minutes find myself by Somerset House and in the Strand, that is to say, in the heart of London. I should then turn to the right, and reach the City, the time- honoured headquarters of finance, shipping, and commerce. To the left lie Charing Cross, and the far-reaching West End, the -seat of rank, wealth, and fashion. I should then pass the Royal Courts of Justice, and thread my way through Fleet-street towards Ludgate-hill, by which I could make a slight ascent to St. Paul's Cathedral, the magnificent architectural con- ception of Sir Christopher Wren. Then I should visit the Mansion House, the official residence of London's chief magistrates; then a short divergence to the left through King. street would lead me to the Guildhall of the City of London. with its small but interesting museum, free library, and art gallery. I should then go and see Trafalgar. Square, with its lofty Nelson Column, national statues, and stately fountains. By turning to the left I should come to the great hotels of Northumberland-avenue, or I could pursue myi way through the memor- able precincts of Whitehall, by the Adiniralty, towards St. James' Park, Westminster Abbey Westminster School, and the Houses a Parlb- ment. I should also visit some more of Ul Interesting places, such as Buckingham Pala:ce, Parade-ground of Hyde Park, Albert Hall, and the old palace of Kensington. -

Parcels are accepted for paroel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for' customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contained in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d.; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4•1.; £2O, 6J.; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 103. MONEY OtIDERS (IfOREION AND COLONIAL.) • The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding 21,31; £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 63. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together xvio cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by td., from GI. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are up to 2s. 6d.; Id. up to 155.; Id. up to 21s. Before patting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to malte yp odd sums.

TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirety, the privilege of transmittiug,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge • for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d., Which covers 12 words, and an additional id. for each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which it charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in Nvall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is 41

The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, a special acknowledgment is sent front the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was,opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REGULATIONS. • Each one must be registered with the councir of a county or county borough, the fee being Li for a motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A registered number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep aftised when driving. Each driver must possess a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car rosy be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dargerous to the public, having regard -to all the circumstances cf the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to the presence of the motor car on the road, the driver must supply his name and address, and the owner and number of the car, tinder heavy penal- ties. The driver must produce his licence at the request of a police constable.

div.head: Alleged Stabbing Affray.
div.p: Alleged Stabbing Affray.

At the Wartington Police Court on Tuesday, Joseph Marratt, joiner, Foundry-street, WAS charged with maliciously cutting and wounding Isabella Manuion at about 8.15 on Monday night. The Chief Coast ible said it would be-necessary to ask for a remand for seven days in order that the woman who was alleged to have been stabbed, could be in attendance. She had been taken to the Infirmary as an inpatient. The doctor informed him (the Chief Constable) that the wound was of a serious natute but not dangerous. There was little doubt that prisoner stabbed her and several women saw him do sq quite clearly. It was stated that he was under the influence of drink at the time.—Priscner said he had no objection to a remand, but he was not guilty.—A remand for a week was granted.

div.head: Landowners and War.
div.p: Landowners and War.

Sir,-1 trust that the strong eppeal made by Mr. R. Ockel may have its effect on the readers of your influential journal. It is not enough that we have Free Trade at our ports. if we are to save the country from anarchy, we must insist on having free production, in the cnly way we can have it, and that is by destroying once for all the land monopoly. If we do not go for- ward and take this step, the Tariff Reformers and the Conscription mongers—the" last ditch "or the landed aristocracy—will plunge us into re-action. As election after election is won by the party of re-action, we can see clearly the trend of things. Free Trade at our ports ' has only lifted us half out of the hole. We can see daylight, but, as workers, we can have no participation in the sunshine of prosperity. All the benefits of good trade go, under existing circumstances, into the pockets of landowners. They are, in the expressive language of Henry George," the robbers that take all that is left,"l after a bare subsistence for the vast majority of our people. The spirit of militarism is spreading. At the instiga- tion of the Minister for War (Mr. Haldane), great corporations like that of Manchester, are offering bribes of 15 days holiday, with full pay, each year to their employees who take service in the Territorialists. Remember that these bribes have to be paid by the other workers, many of whom get no holiday at all— the landowning party pay nothing. Let us repudiate this unjust and wicked method of goading our people into war. We have the means at hand in the taxation of land values. If we insist on landowners paying their quota of taxation—find thus break down the ring which crowds us together in slums and always forces our wages down—we shall once for all put an end to the war spirit which is fomented by the party of privilege. —Yours, &c.,
JOHN B. MIDDLETON.
94, St. Annes-road, E., - - St. Annes-on-the-Sea.

_ Sir Thomas Whittaker anti His Critics. Sir,-Some three months ago I published a pamphlet containing " Some Facts and Arguments " in support of the Licensing Bill. The representatives of the liquor trade have issued a reply which has been pre- pared for them by Mr. F. E. Smith, K.C.' M.P. and Mr Ernest E. Williams. To that reply I will in due course publish a detailed rejoinder. Meanwhile, I shall be glad if you will allow me in your columns, to make some comments upon the criticisms of my critics. The outstanding features of the trade reply are (1) its personal tone with reference to myself ; and (2) its extraordinary omission of any attempt to controvert or even directly attack any fundamental position in my augment. Of petty carping and irrelevant dust-throwing there is abundance, but of serious grappling with the real issues which are before Parliament and the country., there is absolutely none. Indeed, the puerility and futility of the whole production is the greatest com- pliment which has thus far been paid to my parnplet. I Two trained controversialists, both of them barristers, one a K.C., the other a "Fellow of thoßoyalStatisticalj Mr. Andrew liathhone, junr., of Palmer, Massa. div.head: FREE TRADE INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS.
div.p: THE FREE TRADE INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS.
[By C. E. Parker.]

About 500 delegates from all parts of the world have assembled to attend the great International Congress called together by the Cobden Club. Amongst the foreign and Colonial delegates we find representatives from almost every civilised country. Amongst the number are included representatives in the various parliaments of Europe and America, students of political economy, professers from many of the European and American seats of learning, representatives of Chambers of Commerce, &c., &c. It is interesting to see many whose names had been long familiar through their writings. Here are M. Yves Guyot and Paul Beaulier of France ; from !Germany Profeesor Lotz of Munich, Professor IBrandenbury of Berlin, from Hungary the Secretary of the Hungarian Economic Association, and many others who in their own country stand high in both theoretical and practical spheres. We are apt to think that because certain countries are Protectionist, as far as their politics are concerned, their peoples are all Protectionist, that because , Germany as a Protectionist country all Germans must I think this policy the best. A. conference of this sort goes far to remove this impression. The representa- tives from these countries spoke the pure gospel 'of Free Trade, but they by no means spoke 1 as if they were the sole representatives of their faith. There were delegates representing a great body of opinion in their own country, in a minority it is true, but a minority in many cases large and determined which was not for a moment disposed to abandon the fight for freedom of trade as the harbinger of pros- perity, and of peace and goodwill among the nations of the earth. Yecessarily there was a good deal in the addresses which was a re-statement of truths common to all Free Traders, but there were also many statements of facts which were of special interest. For example a German delegate, Dr. Theodore Barth, stated that the working classes of Germany were strong for Free Trade. There is little doubt, if the German franchise was as broad as our own a considerable Free Trade majority would be returned. The German workers have turned their eyes to England with her higher wages, shorter hours, and cheaper living. It would be a great wonder if they did not desire to overturn a system so prejudicial to their class ieterests. A statement by an American delegate, a lawyer from Boston, interested me. He stated that even is America (cramped and dominated as it is by protec- tionist laws), with possibly two exceptions, none of the professors in the seats of learning upheld protection in dealing with economic questions, but the great majority upheld and taught the principles of free exchange as the most profitable for any country. One of our Indian subjects created a favourable impression on the Congress. His strongest point was thern importance of Free Trade to India, especially in connection with our hold on that great dependency. In his opinion the retention of Free Trade between India and the Mother country was the strongest link between the two. Weaken this link, allow India to put on tariffs against the mother country even if such tariffs include preference and you strain to breaking point the bond of union. Whether he be right oe no, I offer no opinion. I restate his opinion because it was evidently the outcome of an observant and intelligent mind. Another point worthy of note was made by Mr. Joseph Martin, K.C. a Canadian delegate. He surprised the Congress by maintaining that in Canada Free Traders were largely in the majority. The farming industry was by far the largest and the farmers were almost to a man free traders ; they returned the present Liberal Government on a Free Trade ticket but it was the Government that had gone wrong. It would have been interesting if he had explained how this had come about. But in regard to preference to Canadian products he was very emphatic. He stated that Canadian farmers had never asked for a preference, they did not require ti preference' and would be too proud to ask for it. He quietly added that if Great Britain in her fancied interests gave a preference they would not refuse it, but the farmers of Canada will never ask for it. The idea that Canadians would stoop to make it the price of their union was absurd. He poured ridicule on the thought of our losing Canada if we do not grant a boon the peoele do not need. " You could not lose us if you would," said ha. The Prime Minister found himself in congenial surroundings on Tuesday night at the banquet of the Hotel Cecil. He was delighted to be associated with men of other nations in a cause whose fortunes he believed to be bound up with the best interests of the world. The " Tariff Reformers "he spoke of as a bed), of gentlemen who have a gift almost amounting to divination for unearthing buried fallacies. Whatever taxation his Government saw reason to adopt would have this feature, it would yield its whole , proceeds to the National Exchequer,and no part would be retained or diverted to serve the particular pur- poses of privileged interests. Keep trade free and open, allow it to follow an unrestricted course along its natural channels,and you will find sooner or later. —and he believed soon rather than later—that it widens and deepens the common stock and goodwill. The characteristic of Asquith's thought and speech is clearness, there is no ambiguity about it. The style is like a Grecian statue, the lines are simple, clear and strong, there is no ornament, no embroidery, but it gives the impression of a strong man with a clear brain, definite conviction, and earnest purpose. It is no small pleasure to see him throw back his massive head, square his shoulders and with a tone of finality declare his conviction that our country would never go back, never teimpose fetters on our greet international commerce, or build tariff walls which are as obsolete as the crumbling castles of the middle ages. The Rt. Hon. Winston Churchill represented the Government in the opening session and the paragraph in his fine speech is worthy of reproduction. Mr. Chat chill said: My noble friend Lord Wolby spoke of Free Trade prospects being overclouded. 1 never was more I confident than lain now of the victory and triumph in this country and all over the world of the ideas ' which we exalt and respect in common. (Cheers.) Which of those two ideas is winning at the present time?. Is it the isolation of nations or their union and their intercourse? Why, with every year that , passes over the globe, with every improvement In communication, with every decision of a Hague tribunal, with every meeting of a Peace Con- 1 ference or an international congress of any sort or i kind, the unity of the civilised world and the inter- relation and interdependence of all civilised modern communities is being steadily and irresistibly advanced. (Cheers.) Yes, in spite of the folly of , armaments and tariffs, in spite of ths unwisdorn of ' so many of our political and journalistic hotheads, the unity and solidarity of the civilised world grows stronger from year to year and almost from month to month. (Cheers.) " All the men," as Diderot said, " in all the lands have become neces- sary to one another." (Cheers.) And this process of consolidation and amalgamation which is going irresistibly forward, which is in the centre of the whole movement of the modern world, is taking place without the slightest loss of national tradi- tions, of love of national characterhtics, of the culture and development of each community in itself and for itself. ,On the contrary, as mankind has become more united and civilised, you have found that study of the past, that introspective examination by each race of its own history, of its own innate characteristics, which everywhere is producing a great and harmless growth of peace- I ful nationalism within the larger internationalism of the world. (Cheers.) - I was glad to hear the letter from Win. Lloyd Garrison, son of the great liberApr, read to us by an American representative urging that the question should be lifted on to the moral plane. It is very much on the same lines as a letter I got from Garrison some months back, and it is a point I have myself tried to urge.. There are many minds so limited in their build and range as to be quite unable to follow the deduc- tive reasoning which from an economic standpoint makes for Free Trade a position which cannot be shaken, but these same individuals are often thoroughly alive and sensitive on the moral side, and ready to respond to the moral issuo. We must "hitch the waggon to the stars." Lloyd Garrison's letter eentained the following : If I were to be present I should urge concentra- tion on the iniquity of Protection rather than upon its inexpediency. The statistical and economic injury and waste of the system have been exposed a thousand times from Adam Smith down to date. The arguments rwely change convictions. The wisdom and power of the anti-slavery movement were shown in its refusal to discuss expedients and in its unceasing assertion of fundamental principles. It is easier to touch conscience than to inform the understanding. I hoped to be present at the gather- ing simply to arraign Protection tic a device for enthroning privilege, corrupting Government, debasing public morals, cultivating the war spirit,

Mr. Eastham further con- 'tended that the applicant, having taken so much I drink as to cause him to dose, was guilty of serious
4s::e

and wilful misconduct. j The Judge, in summing up. said he was of the opinion from the evidence that applicant was sober at the time of the accident, and his view was borne out by indepen- dent testimony. It was clear that the applicant was ' sent to High Legh by the respondent to fetch the pigs, and therefore the accident happened in the course of his employment. Moreover, Grounds was a driver and not an amateur, and there was no misconduct on the part of the applicant in handing him the reins. His Honour awarded the applicant 15s. a week during incapacity, from the date of the accideat,with costs on scale B
MR. ALLAN WILKIE NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. RETURN VISIT OF MR. ALLAN WILKIE.

Next week the lovers of Shakespeare in Warrington will have an opportunity of witnessing the perform- ances of the eminent tragedian Allan Wilkie, who will grace the boards of the Court Theatre. Mr. Wilkie played leading parts with several of the principal London actor-managers including Mr. Beerbohm Tree, Mr. Fred Terry, and Miss Julia Neilson, etc., with enormous success, but all his past successes paled into insignificance when some three years ago he made his debut as a Shakespearean star. Since then his career has been veritably a triumphal progress through the provinces, and we have to go back to the days of Barry Sullivan to find a parallel to the wildly enthusi- astic receptions lie has met with hi every town he has visited. In such large centres as Liverpool, Nottingham, Manchester, Birmingham, and at the Theatre Royal, Bradford, packed houses have been a nightly occurenee. The reason for this is not far- to seek —Mr. Wilkie is possessed of a compiling power and intensity such as can be found in no other con- temporary Shakespearean actor, and compared with the degenerate, milk and water methods of the present school, his concentrated earnestness and tragic intensity comes as a positive revelation to the present generation of play goers, combining as he does all the best traditions of the old school with the naturalness and po'ish of the present. His Shylock, Othello, and Richard certainly have no superiors on the British stage to-day, and his Hamlet has many points of originality and interest, and above all the supreme gift of youthfulness in which quality so many Hamlets are piiinfully lacking. Nor is the Company headed by Mr. Wilkie by any means a " one-man show "—he has gathered round him an exceptionally talented company of over 35 artistes including Miss Carrie Millie, who played the leading parts with the late Osmond Tearle, and who is undmhtedly one of the most charming actresses in the country ; Mr. Alexander Marsh, who played the entire leads in the Osmond Tearle Company subse- quent to that gentleman's decease ; Mr. Frank Royde, for many years associated with Mr. Beerbohm Tree at His Majesty's Theatre ; Hr. John Payley, the principal support to Mr. Barry Sullivan on his farewell tours; Mr. lan Fleming, an inimitable Shakespearean comedian, &c. The bill for the week is :—Monday, "The Merchant of Venice" ; Tuesday, " Othello" ; Wednesday, " Richard III." ; Thursday, "Romeo and Juliet Friday, " The Sleigh Bells" and "David Garrick Saturday, " Hamlet."

div.head: BANKRUPT APPLIES FOR DISCHARGE Official Receiver and Under-Estimating
div.p: BANKRUPT APPLIES FOR DISCHARGE Official Receiver and Under-Estimating
for Contracts.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.C, Mr. T. S. Steel applied on behalf of Charles Ellison Chappel, of Alexandra-road, Stockton Heath, for his discharge from bankruptcy.—Mr. Johnson, assistant official receiver, read the official receiver's report from which it appeared that according to the bankrupt's statement of affairs (submitted on 19th August 1903) the liabilities to rank for dividend were estimated as £9OO 4s. id., but the proofs actually admitted at this date (R,791 10s. Id.) and the probable claims not yet proved (£524 155.) ' amounted to £1,316 ss. id. This marked difference between the estimated and the actual and probable liabili- ties (2426 Is.) was due mainly to the fact that the bank- Irupt under-estimated some of the liabilities he disclosed and omitted four amounting in the aggregate to £386 2s. 4d. The assets, so far as they were not assigned to ' creditors wholly or partially secured, were estimated to produce £l3l 12s. 2d., but they had realized only IRIO 9s. 53. This -considerable difference was mainly , accounted for by the fact that the two largest book debts estimated to realise £99 • 12s. were covered by ' contra accounts and, therefore, should not have been included as assets. The balance available for costs and distribution among unsecured creditors was £3B 18s. sd. instead of £125 9s. Bd., as estimated by the bankrupt. No dividend whatever had been or could be paid to unsecured creditors. The bankrupt commenced business as a builder and contractor at Fairfield-road, Stockton Heath, in the year 1853, in partnership with Mr. Thomas Millington, without capital. Mr. Millington retired on 13th December, 1901, receiving £IS in cash and about £ls's worth of goods for so doing.No formal partnership accounts were taken at or prior to the dissolution, but the bankrupt nod his partner endeavoured to arrive approximately at the financial position of the firm, and the conclusion they arrived at was that the firm was slightly insolvent —that there was an excess of liabilities of £2l. That being so, the payment of £3O to the retiring partner did not seem to have been justifiable. The bankrupt. however, appeared to have thought there was a good- will in the business and that if he were entitled to all the profits arising therefrom, be could earn a fair livelihood. His expectations, however, were far from being justified inasmuch as the business of tho period covered by the bankrupt's solo trading had not attained even that moderate measure of success it appeared to have done during the partnership. The main cause con- tributing to the insolvency was the bankrupt's persistent loss on contracts due either to bad luck or bad judgment. On the whole it seemed difficult to avoid the conclusion that the business lost more by the withdrawal of Mr. Millington's experience and skill than it gained by being relieved of one partner. A considerable porta() of the public examination was directed towards a transfer by the bankrupt of his interest in an uncompleted contract to a Mr. Pemberton in consideration of-a loan; it was also suggested that the bankrupt had moved materials intended for one house to another. The official receiver was of opinion that although the matters in question were proper subjects for inquiry there was nothing in them so derogatory to the bankrupt's character or conduct as a trader as to justify any submission thereon. The bank- rupt kept a fair set of books and probably the true explanation of his conduct and trading was his lack of means at the commencement of his sole trading. The bankrupt's operations, although far from being insignifi- cant, were not on a very largo scale, or he might hate caused serious loss and distress to a large body of creditors, but the official receiver submitted that systematic under-estimating contracts was a most repre- hensible practice, since not only did it prevent the perroa who engaged in .the contract from paying his creditors, but it also injured traders who conducted their business on legitimate lines by under-selling them. The conduct of the bankrupt during the bank- ruptcy had been satisfactory. Mr. Steel said the bankrupt had been unfortunate in busin^ss. He had disclosed the whole of his estate and had given every assistance to the official receiver. He suggested that the bankrupt be granted the dis- charv, subject to the minimum period of two years' suspension. His Honour granted the application on the above condition.

The State of Trade. An extraordinary general meeting of Parr's Bank, Limited, was held at the Bank Premises, Winwick- street, Warrington, at noon on Tbursday. Mr. Cecil F. Parr (chairman of directors) presided, and there were also present :—Sir J. Christopher Gamble, Bart., the Hon. Arthur Stanley, M.P., Messrs. Thomas H. Dixon' N. Ffarrington Eckersley, Alfred Hewlett, Robert Neill, Hassey Paoke, and Alfred Morrison Turner .(directors), Frank Hudson, E. C. Cooper,Peter Gratrix, A. W. Newton, R. Barbour, Wallace Broadbent, Charles Baker, ChPrles White, John Pakeman, James Barber, E. Lewis-Littler, R. C. Fletcher W. Booth, John Coxon, John White,R. Pierpoint,J. al'akinson,George Leicester, Rowland Young. J. D. Buokton, Robert DAson, T. Smith, C. T. Wilifley, D. Goldsworth, W. Mitchell, Joel Wainwright, Dr. Brindle, William Morris, W, Skinner, C. E. Steen, O. Cockraine, J. A. McGregor. W. Silcock, James Lees, Joseph Hughson, W. Atherton, Hy. Dean A. Lister Kaye,' H. Percy Mortimer, Jos. Johnson, 'W. Mitchell, W. B. Houghton, Miss Emma Davies, (shareholders), R. W. Whalley (general manager), and E. D. Hyatt (secretary.) MR. PARR'S SPEECH. The CHAIRMAX, in moving the adoption of the report of the directors, which has already appeared in the i" Examiner," explained that the reason why the meeting I was being held a week later than usual was that they I had recently, after somewhat protracted negotiations, I acquired the business of an old-established bank in I Jersey, and Mr. Whalley and-the deputy chairman (Mr. 'Fraser) were only able to go over to the island last ' week to complete the purchase. The bank they had acquired—Messrs. Robin's—had • been carried on by members of the same family for just one hundred years, and the two brothers of that name who wore now hand- ing it over were willing to continue to give the bank all their influence and support. Continuing, Mr. Parr said that in January last he characterissd the growing decrease in

div.head: VOLUME OF TRADE
div.p: THE VOLUME OF TRADE

ass set back from theprevious unprecedented expansion rather than as the beginning of a wholesale and continued depression. He was bold enough to be still much of the same opinion. It was quite true that one read frequently enough in the papers of the shutting down of iron works or of short time in the textile industries and individual instances certainly were com- mon, showing a depression which it was rather difficult perhaps to explain away. But if they looked at the figures in the lump be thought they certainly went far towards giving them a more hopeful view of the situa- tion in the immediate future. Everyone, he was sure, would agree that trade was exceptionally and almost nniversally good in the first - five months of the year 1907. It was a record and during that time the exports of Great Britain came to the sum of £161,010,030. And yet, for the five months ending June last, notwith- standing all the depression,those same exports amounted to £149,000,000 which, after all, was a small drop Lam a record year of 7 per cent. Moreover that £149,000,000 would have been a record in itself if it had not been eclipsed by the still larger figures of the year before. Again, to take a different test, in times of great depression failures increased and liquidations and bankruptcies abounded. But what were the facts? Daring the extraordinarily prosperous year ending June 1907 the total number of bankruptcies and liquidations in Great Britain was 9,716, and yet in the following year, ending June last, when we were supposed to be going from bad to worse and is a state of great depression, the number was only 9,774—a difference of 61, which was merely an ircrease of 6 per cont. Therefore he thought he was justified in saying that in some parts the stories of depression might be somewhat exaggerated. Ho thought that as soon as the large stocks which had been left over from the piping times of the early months of last year had been worked off—he feared it might be sacrificed, in many instances, at lower prices—we could look for a healthier ratio between supply and demand and,he hoped, a corresponding improvement in trade. They must not forget that during the last six months no less than £116,000,000 had been raised in London alone, most of it for the promotion of new or the extension of old enterprises all over the world. That enormous sum was already carrying interest and could not be allowed to lie idle. Its gradual expenditure on industrial propositions must already have began and must therefore be exercising a potent influence in stimulating and broadening the markets of the world, our own included. To turn to the WASTE SHEET, although they brought forward from their December balance sheet some £lO,OOO more than they did six months ago, namely, £158,000 as against £148,000, they presented the shareholders with a profit for the half- year of £359,000 in round figures, which was some £B,OOO less than they showed last January. Of course, if they compared it with the June half of last year— end that was really the legitimate comparison to make, because there was a difference in the two half-years—they would find the profits were £1,500 less. When they considered the relative value of money as well is the demand for it as between one half year and the other, they were quite satisfied—and more than satisfied—with the results they showed. He hoped the shareholders after studying - the balance sheet sufficiently would be satisfied not only with the amount of profit made, but with the way in which the directors asked them to allocate it. He was sure, first of all, they would approve of the dividend of 19 per cent as usual. He bad received a letter from a shareholder bearing an old name in Warrington—that of Buckton—asking why they could not pay 25 per cent instead of 19 per cent and bonus. The directors had often discussed that question and had come to the conclusion that it was better to go on as they were. He did not want to begin paying 20 per cent and then have to come down to 19 again. Their movements forward had always been characterised by great prudence and he thought the shareholders would agree that it would be better to look at that matter from a conservative point of view and that so long as they got their money it really did not matter what they called it. He was sure they would approve the piping of the customary amounts of £15,000 to the previous account and £15,000 to the Officers' Superannuation Fund. No body of men had served an institution better than their staff served Parr's Bank. (Hear, hear). During the second half-year of 1907, continued Mr. Parr, they kept themselves, from prudential motives,

UNUSUALLY STRONG in the matter of cash and surplus funds, although at that time money was in demand and rates were high and tempting. This half-year their position had possibly been even stronger but from quite a different reason. They had had perforce to keep their money in hand because they could net find people who wanted to borrow it. Even what they did lend, was not lent at a very remunerative rate. On the very day of their meeting at Cannon-street six months ago the bank rate dropped from 5 per cent. to 4, and money had been getting cheaper ever since. They found themselves ending up tha six months with the bank rate at 21, and possibly money at a lower value still. He would like to point out that gilt-edged securities which, especially in consols, they held to a large extent, had in the aggregate appreciated in value during the last six months. The price of consols alone had appreciated to the extent of 4 points—from 831 to 871, the price on July Ist. He was sorry to say that now it had gone back to 861, but still that was an improvement on the 831 of last year Further, the rise could not be regarded as a set off in the matter of the half year's profit, because they never reckoned such appreciation into their profits, though they bad frequently• used their profits to cover depreciation, and hence it was that their investments were always held at a figure very considerably below their market value. The total amount of their investments, compared with their last balance sheet, was some £950,000 larger. They were unable to lend out their proper proportion of funds to customers, so they had recourse to placing it in good, safe securities which, owing to the favourable conditions prevailing, they were able to buy at a profitable figure and which, while yield- ing a very fair rate of interest, were not likely to increase in capital value. Many of thorn, too, were short-dated securities, and thus would fall for repay- ment during the time when they hoped trade conditions rai,ght be better, and then they would be able to use the money in the ordinary course of their business. lie ought to draw attention to an addition to THE AUDITOR'S REPORT, which now stated We have audited the above balance sheet and have obtained all the information and explana- tions we have required. In our opinion such balance sheet is properly drawn up so as to exhibit a true and correct view of the state of the company's affairs, according to lho best of our information and the explanations given us and as shown by the books of the Company." Those words had been inserted in obedience to the requirements of the new Companies Act which came into operation on the Ist July last. They had followed the exact words of the clause of the Act and that must be their sufficient excuse for the unnecessary repetition and the clumsiness of the wording, for which the directors must not be held responsible. (Laughter.) lie used hardly say that the auditors of Parr, s Bank from the very first year of the company's existence had always readily obtained all the information and explana- tion that they could possibly require. Some six months ago he was prec!uded from alluding, it being then sub- jadiß, to an

div.head: ACTION FOR LIBEL
div.p: ACTION FOR LIBEL

..... brought by the bank against the editor and publisher of a certain paper called" Vanity Fair." That paper had taken up the cause of a certain IHr. Horsfall, a former customer of the Alliance Bank, who had attacked the bank in a most violent manner in a series of pamphlets. Tho result of tho action was a complete vindication of the bank's good name in open Court and a judgment for £5,000, doubly confirmed by the Court of Appeal in strong and unmistakable language. Having pointed out that the directors were carryink forward .£167,000, as against £158,000 last year, Mr. Parr con- cluded by formally moving the adoption of the report and the declaration of a dividend of 19 per cent, per annum, payable, free of income tax, on ugust 711. Mr. T. 11. DIXON seconded and the motion was unanimously passed.

div.head: WARRINGTON AGRICULTURAL BOGIE TY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AGRICULTURAL BOGIE TY.

The Warrington and District Agricultural Society will hold its annual shat" in Walton Park, on Thursday next, and only fine weather is needed to assure its success. Prizes, cups, &-;.. are offered to the value of about £7OO. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., ia again the President. There are classes for shires, hunters, hackneys, harness horses, jumpers, tradesmen's or tenant Canners' turnouts, cattle, pigs, cheese and butter. Entry forms and all particulars may be obtained from Mr. H. Beresford Melville, Bold-street, Warrington. Sir Gilbert Greenall offers three cups for competition, Mr. F. Stapleton Bretherton a special prize value £5, the Execntors of the late Colonel R. Pilkington, Mr. Joseph Palmer, Lymm, Mr. John Coxon and Mr. A. B. Boumphteys, Lymm, silver cups, Mr. J. Whittaker Kenworthy, Mr. James Gould, the Warrington Shire Horse Society, the Cheshire Hunt Covert Fund, Messrs. Henry Milling and Co., Messrs. Day and Sons, and Messrs. Barmak, Limited, special prize. Models are also offered by the Shire Horse Society, the Hunters' Improvement Society, and the Hackney Horse Society. Sir Gilbert Greenall gives premiums of £3 in some of the tenant farmer classes. In connection with the show will be held the third Walton Flower Show and cottage garden prize competi- tion. This is a most attractive feature of the show in which Lady Greenall is particularly interested, For two or three years the Band of the Yorkshire Hussars has played a selection of music at the Show. There will be a change this year, the famous Karoly Klays Imperial Blue Hungarian Band having been engaged. 'Visitors to the show may look forward with confidence to a rich musical treat; even if not keenly interested in the show itself.

div.p: County Court Sequel.
DIRECTORS THANKED.

Mr. Rorirra—Prz-a—Po—n7m—o -ve7d7v-rte—of thinks to the directors for their services during the past halfl year. He said he bad the honour of moving a similar:, vote of thanks at a meeting at Cannon-street six months , ago and he then remarked that the spassity of attendance of shareholders was in Itself a compliment to the ability of the directors. It was the privilege), " of one who proposed a complimentary resolution such as that to take the argument the other „- way if he chose, and his argument that da3:-, was that the comparatively large attendance °LI., shareholders in Warrington was an obvious compliment, to the directors for the way in which they had con-, ducted the business. (Laughter and hear, hear.) They -• were particularly indebted to Mr. Parr for his attend- ance, for it was evident that, suffering from a cold as he was, it was only hiS devotion to duty which made hint come to the meeting. Mr. JOHN WHITE seconded and the vote was heartily accorded. The CHarnmAtq in reply said the directors always tried to do their beet for the bank. OFFICERS THANKED. ' The Hon. ARTHUR STANLEY, M.P., moved a vote of thanks to the general manager, assistant general manager, managers, secretary and other officers of the bank for their services during the half-year. He said the directors who had the good fortune to be associated with Mr. Whalley in his work were fully satisfied that in him they had got the best general manager of any bank in the kingdom. (gear, hear.) They wen also glad to know that that opinion was shared by all those who in the course of business came ii touch with him. It was obvious that in a large,increas- in.' business like theirs, the work of the assistant general manager must be very heavy, and all credit should be given to that officer for the way in which he carried it out. M regarded the staff, he was glad to hoar the Chairman say that no staff could possibly servo better or more loyally than the staff of Parr's Bank. Mr. J. Coxos seconded and the vote was unanimously , passed. Mr. WHALLEY, in acknowledging the compliment. said be could only repeat what he had previously said in that room—that they had got a thoroughly loyal staff who did their bast in the interests of the bank and who were just as pleased as the shareholders with the success they had attained. NEW DEPARTURES. The CHAIRMAN said they had been asked by morer,i, than one customer lately whether they intended, as - some banks had already done, to take up the duties of trustees. As they thought it might prove atonveni- ence to many of those who had already had business relations with the bank, the directors were asking the meeting to sanction a formal application for the necessary power. It was quite conceivable that man I people might have less compunction in asking a publi body which had neither a soul to save nor a body to kick, to act for them rather than impose on their friends what was often regarded as a thankless and troublesome duty. They did not at present know how mach labour would be involved, but their custom ers might rest assured that any charge they might have to make would be strictly on the side of moderation. He moved that the provisions of the Memorandum of Association of the company be altered to enable the bank to take over the duties.

• The CHAIRMAN then moved that the following article be substituted for article 17 : "The company may by special resolution sub-divide its shares or any of them." The directors, he said, hid considered the question for many years and they had now come to the conclusion that the present size of the individual share, with a very large nominal liability attaching to it, did certainly act as a deterrent to the small and possibly the very prudent investor in bank shares. If their shares were £5O each and £l.O paid, he felt convinced there would be a readier and steadier market for them. As things were now, if £lOO or £2OO shares were thrown on the market from some deceased shareholder's estate there was, owing to the very large liability and the size of the shares, a restricted demand for them and all the shares were depressed in value through no fault of their own. The directors had no hesitation in advising the shareholders to sanction the alteration. fie 'lid not say they had any intention of putting it into immediate practice, and if they wished to use the power they would have to obtain the shareholders' consent.
On the motion of Mr. JOITX PAICEMAN, seconded hv Mr. JoEr. WAINWRIGHT, a vote of thanks was passed Co the Chairman for presiding.,

div.head: PALACE AND -HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND -HIPPODROME.

The management of this up-to-date place of amusement present their patrons with another admirable programme this week and large audiences have manifested unmistakable appreciation. First on the bill comes Jack Pleasants, a comedian with a distinct style of his own, who convulses the audience with his amusing songs and droll ways. He gives three numbers—" I'll be cross," "I've never been in lodgings before," "Fur 14s. GI a week," and merri- ment reigns supreme whilst he is on the stage, Margit and Loner, continental eccentrics, present a turn which is not only exceedingly laughable but bears the stamp of originality. Both performers are skilled acrobats and tumblers and keep things decidedly lively for teri minutes or so. One of the most pleasing features of the programme is Hanid Alexander's novel entertain- ment at the piano. his young lady not only demon- strates great skill as a pianist by her performance of a transcription of "For all eternity," but sings a very taking ditty entitled "Jest her way, and also gives a realistic recital descriptive of the impressions of two city youngsters , who were taken for an outing in the country. Ethel Sheffer's illu- strated songs form a popular item and special mention should be made of the Faceograph, introduced for the first time in this country, which is a novel inven- tion, meeting with general approval. Our readers should not miss the opportunity of seeing this—the latest thing in the way of entertainment. Barry Nelson, quaint comedian, scores a great success with a smart skit "My wife's a suffingette " and is rewarded with many a round of hearty applause. ...- Matthews - and Brown, up-to-date comedians and 1-, dancers, are experts in their line of business, their dancing being exceptionally clever. Mdllet. • Bartenelli, contortionist, performs some amazio,g feats, while Dunn and Beano are skilful ec-centric- • parody acrobats. Raymond's Bio Tableaux show a , laughable set entitled " Father ill-uses Gussie b The -, entertainment is interesting and enjoyable throughout, and well repays patronage. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Another very attractive bill is announced for next week. The premier position is taken by the Royal entertainers, the Gothams, vocalists and comedians, who will present a capital turn. Dave Samuels, tho great American Hebrew comedian' will appaar, and the other artistes will be : —Little Dolly Brougb, the juvenile favourite ; Les Frasettis, in their refined musical act; Jim Obeetharn, king of boy whistlers and bird mimicry ; Billy French, the stylish wooden shoe dancer; Gravetta and Parr, American novelty artistes ; Gold and Sterling in "The Welsh girl and the artist," a refined musical comedy and speciality scene.

WARRINGTON WOMAN'S SUICIDE. The Coroner and the Police. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at Warrington yesterday touching the death of Mary Kirk: (11), Admiral-street, Warrington. The evidence showed that on Tuesday night deceased was seen by a girl named Winifred Flynn to drink something from a bottle and a neighbour,Margaret Lawton, afterwards found her lying in a dying condition on the sofa. She was taken to the Infirmary but died on the way. It appeared that earlier in the day deceased purchased a bottle ni carbolic acid from Charles .7. Chamberlain, chemist, Church-street,and she then appeared to be quite rational. P.C. Dennett stated tir.A he received information of the occurrence at 10 o'clock on Wednesday morning. II? visited the house and detected a strong smell 01- carbolic acid.

The Coroner: Are you aware that information of this death was given to one of the police sergeants at 10 o'clock on Tuesday night ? Witness : Yes, sir. The Coroner then remarked that it was very probable that that inquest could have been held on WednesdaY when he was holding an inquest on a boy who vos drowned, and mace grief and pain could have beer spared to the relatives. The case was reported at ten o'clock on Tuesday night and in any other part of Oa county tho inquest would have been held and the evidence have been ready on Wednesday. There were fourteen hours between the time the police got to kne',. of the matter and the time when ha held the ioques" on too boy. lie wrote to the Chief Constable asking why the case could not be got together Or Wednesday, and he received a reply stating that the sergeant who was informed of the death P,rc'i,; ceded to the house and returned with only a t facts, that the case was incomplete and he did think it could hare been properly got togother f°,e' Wednesday. lie (the Coroner) was saving this gni' calmly and cooly : he could not possibfy carry out the, duties of his office in South-West Lancashire liole7 the police co-operated with him. There was no part c;„ South West Lancashire except Warrington where ,ti!Jf case could not have been prepared for him for 12.2 d Wednesday. The Puy returned a verdict of " Suicide whilst of unsound mind."

For the brass Mud contest six bands entered for prizes aggregating £55, but only one (Crosfield's Warrington) appeared, and to them was awarded the first prize. Conductor, Mr. G. F. Bedforth. Fatal Accident at Warburton. . On Wednesday a party from Nelson's, Liverpool, were picnicing at the Saracen's Head, Warburton. i One of the party was trying the aerial flight, when al companion, Cunningham by name, wished to join , him. "I'm coining with you," he said. The other , replied," Nay, Icannot take us both." Cunningham, disregarding this clung on to his companion, and, ' losing his hold, fell to the ground, breaking his neck. He leaves a widow and five children. , Children's Summer Camp. • The first batch of boys under the charge of If r. and Mrs. Cox and officers arrived at Prestatyn on Saturday at 11 30 a.m. They number 103. The week in camp has been thoroughly enjoyed for in addition to the usual rambles through a charming district,aports have been engaged in with zest. The children returned to 'Warrington last evening, leaving Prestatyn at 7.3 p.m. The cookin,g arrangements have been excellently carried out by Mr. and Mrs. Whitney and Miss E. Bostock. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANO.A.SHIRE.—AdVE, Cheshire Acres Wanted for Small Holdings. In presenting the minutes of the Small Holdings and Allotments Committee at the Cheshire County Council on Thursday, Mr. E. G. Leycester said that negotia- tions for the Crown lands at Delamere had fallen through, as the Crown could not accept the Council's terms. The commissioners for the Crown proposed themselves to carve out the land into small holdings, and applications had been passed as satisfactory for nearly 2,000 acres. The purchase had been made by the Council of 850 acres in Ledsham, which the coin- mittee would proceed to deal with as soon as possible in order to settle some of the applicants upon the land' Prosecutor Does hot Appear. At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, bef ,re Mr. H. Roberts and other magistrates, a little girl named Annie Johnson, of Utkinton, Cheshire, pleaded not guilty to stealing two bead necklets and a brooch, valued at Is. 4d. from a stall in the Market-place, the property of Sol Sumpter, of Cheethaan, Manchester.— The Chairman said that as the prosecutor did not appear, he thought the case ought to be dismissed. Ile didalot think they ought to depart from the practice of the Court. —The Chief Constable said it was no uae for the police to detect these cases if they collapsed in this way,—The Chairman said the;r feelings were with the girl and she would Ze dismissed. LAWN TENNIS, CROQUET AND GARDEN REQuisrrEe.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge- street, Warrington.—Advt. Wedding at Sankey. St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, was the scene of a very pretty wedding on Monday afternoon when Mr. Joseph Richardson, of Palk View, Peeketh, was married to Amelia, the only daughter of Mr. William Hughes, Station-road, Penketh. The bride was given away by her father and was attired in a pretty dove grey dress. She wore a charming white crinoline hat sun carried a banquet of carnations and roses. The Rev. J. R. Jones, M.A., performed the ceremony, after which a reception wa.slield at the bride's house. Mr. James Hughes -discharged the duties of best mm. Later in the day the happy couple left for Holywell for their honeymoon. They received many useful presents. The Street Improvement Committee has resolved, that the Town Clerk apply to the Looal Government Beard for an order to put in force the compulsory powers of the Lands' Clauses Act with regard to the widening of Butterinarket-street and tho acquisition of other pro, parties in the Bororgh. A Neglectful Husband. John Barry, 18, Gandy's-terrace, Warrington, pleaded guilty at the Borough Court, on Thursday, to a charge of neglecting to maintain his wife and children, whereby they became chargeable to the Union.—Mr. Basil Shearer prosecuted, and stated that the prosecutor had been previously convicted of a similar offence. Prisoner's wife and two children were admitted to the Workhouse on July 28th in con- sequence of Op prisoner's neglect to maintain them. ! —Prisoner was sent to gaol for three mouths.

Dutton being second rith.l49. CRUSADE AGAINST STREET BETTING. Maximum Penalties Inflicted. At the %Carrington Pollee Court, on Tuesday, Joseph Lawreuson, Forster-street, was charged with loitering at the rear of Houghton-street at about 1.30 on Monday afternoon for the purpose of betting, and with loitering at the rear of Bluecont-street for a similar offence on July 3rd.—Mr. Steel appeared for tLe prisoner, and pleaded guilty to both charges. The Chief Constable stated that Constable Holland and Woolacett kept observation between 1.15 and 1.33 on Monday, and during that time they saw prisoner receive three slips, which appeared to contain money, and then they arrested him. He had in his possession 12 slips relating to betting transactions upcnThorses running at Sandown Park, Ripon, and Birmingham, a sporting newspaper, and a paying out slip. On Friday the same of:leers saw him receive between 12.13 p.m. and 2.5 p.m, 23 bets from 13 men, nine women, three girls, and two boys. A number of other people went to prisoner, but the officer could not say v;hether they handed him slips or not. Mr. Steel said prisouer did this sort of thing out of sheer necessity. Some seven years ago, he met with a serious accident. He was trapped by a train, and his right leg was very badly, smashed and ho lost three fingers on his left hand. Fle was in the Warrington Infirmary for two years. Owing to his injured leg he had been unable to obtain employment, and he Lad ins.tructcd him (Mr. Steel) that he bad bad no corn-' pensation at all. Prisoner would promise he would drcp this sort of thing. He was a poor man, and having regard to all the circumstances, he thought it was a case which should be placed under the Probation of Offenders Act. The Chairman said the maximum fines would be inflicted,£lo and costs in each case(£2o 10s.altogether), with the alternative of two months' imprisonment.
